role: Software CRC-32/MPEG-2 implementation for the bootloader: single-shot, chunked-accumulate (used during DFU WRITE to build a running CRC then compared in VERIFY), and a flash-region CRC helper used by the app-image integrity check before jumping to the application.
compiled_in: Bootloader standalone binary only (linked @0x08033000). Not part of the APP/BOARD/COMM firmware matrix; the whole Bootloader/ tree compiles into one image regardless of APP/BOARD. Every function is referenced from bl_main.c / bl_dfu.c, so the translation unit is live in that single build.

findings.description: bl_crc32_flash validates only start_addr against [0x08000000, 0x08040000) but never bounds start_addr + length_bytes. A large length_bytes (or start near the top of flash) makes bl_crc32_calculate read past 0x08040000 (end of flash) into reserved/option/peripheral address space. There is also an unchecked uint32 overflow: start_addr + length_bytes can wrap. The function is a public API and carries no caller-side guarantee.
findings.impact: Over-read past flash end during app integrity verification. In the sealed deployment this is reached via bl_validate_app_crc(header) with header->app_size taken from the on-flash app header. The only thing preventing the over-read today is that bl_validate_app_header() caps app_size<=APP_MAX_SIZE and pins app_start_addr==APP_FLASH_BASE BEFORE the CRC is computed — but that ordering lives in the caller, not here. If a corrupt/garbage header is ever CRC-checked without that prior cap (e.g. a future caller, or header validation reordered), the bus access past flash end can fault/hang the bootloader, which on a sealed unit means no recovery.
findings.recommendation: Add an end-bound + overflow check inside bl_crc32_flash: reject if length_bytes > (0x08040000 - start_addr), i.e. compute the remaining span as a uint32 and compare, before casting start_addr to a pointer. Return 0 on violation as the existing range failure does.

findings.description: Static flag crc_initialized is write-only: set true in bl_crc_init (line 28), set false in bl_crc_deinit (line 34), but never read anywhere in the file or project. bl_crc_deinit's only effect is mutating this dead flag. None of the CRC functions guard on initialization, so init/deinit are effectively no-ops aside from bl_crc_init resetting crc_state (which bl_crc_reset already does).
findings.impact: No functional bug, but it implies an init/lifecycle contract that does not exist — a reader may assume calling accumulate without init is rejected (it is not). Minor code rot / false safety signal.
findings.recommendation: Either remove crc_initialized and make bl_crc_deinit a documented no-op (or delete it), or actually enforce it: have bl_crc32_accumulate/get return a defined sentinel or assert when !crc_initialized. Removing is simplest given the bootloader never calls deinit.

findings.description: CRC accumulate/verify domain mismatch. In bl_dfu_cmd_write, flash is written with 0xFF-padded data (aligned_len, bl_dfu.c:233-246) but the running CRC is accumulated over only the unpadded payload: bl_crc32_accumulate(payload, payload_len) (bl_dfu.c:262). The final image is then re-CRC'd over the whole padded flash span via bl_crc32_flash(app_start, app_size) in bl_validate_app_crc (bl_main.c:730). If any WRITE chunk has payload_len not a multiple of 8, the accumulated DFU CRC (over unpadded bytes) and the flash CRC (over padded bytes, including injected 0xFF) cover different byte streams and will not match the same expected value. The two CRC consumers (DFU VERIFY at bl_dfu.c:315 vs boot-time validate at bl_main.c:730) therefore disagree on what 'the CRC' is.
findings.impact: For aligned/full chunks (the normal host case) both agree, so this can pass all bench tests and still be a latent integrity hole: a tool that sends a final short unpadded chunk produces a flash image whose boot-time CRC differs from the DFU-accepted CRC. Worst case a unit accepts a DFU that the boot validator later rejects (boot loop) or vice-versa. On a sealed unit this is a brick risk.
findings.recommendation: Make the accumulated CRC cover exactly the bytes written to flash: accumulate aligned_data over aligned_len (matching bl_flash_write), so the running CRC equals bl_crc32_flash over the same padded span. Add a unit test asserting accumulate-over-padded == flash-CRC for a non-8-aligned final chunk.

findings.description: The unit test does NOT exercise bl_crc.c. It defines a private copy of crc32_byte/crc32_calculate inside the test file and tests that copy. The shipped symbols (bl_crc32_calculate, bl_crc32_accumulate, bl_crc32_get, bl_crc_init/reset, bl_crc32_flash, and the NULL/length==0 guards) have zero direct coverage. The algorithm copy can stay correct while bl_crc.c regresses and the suite still passes.
findings.impact: False confidence: 'CRC32 tests pass' does not mean the bootloader CRC code is correct. The accumulate state machine, the flash range/overflow guard, and the NULL guards are all untested in the real code path — exactly the areas with the findings above.
findings.recommendation: Link the real bl_crc.c into the test target and test the public API directly: accumulate equivalence (chunked == single-shot), reset/get state, NULL/zero-length returns, and bl_crc32_flash range rejection (with flash address mocked). Keep the known test vector 0x0376E6E7 against bl_crc32_calculate.

findings.description: Ambiguous overloaded return value: bl_crc32_calculate and bl_crc32_flash return 0 both for the error case (NULL/length==0/bad range) and as a legitimate CRC result (0 is a valid CRC-32/MPEG-2 output for some inputs). bl_crc32_accumulate returns crc_state on (NULL||length==0) which is a no-op — a different convention from the other two. Callers cannot distinguish 'computation failed' from 'CRC happens to be 0'.
findings.impact: bl_validate_app_crc (bl_main.c:730-732) treats a 0 from a rejected range as just a CRC value; it would compare 0==header->app_crc32 and could spuriously pass if a header ever declared app_crc32==0. Low likelihood given header validation, but the API shape invites the mistake.
findings.recommendation: Document the 0-on-error overload in the header, or change the API to out-param + bool status. At minimum note in bl_crc.h that callers must validate inputs before relying on the result, and ensure bl_validate_app_crc never treats app_crc32==0 as valid.

findings.description: Flash window bounds 0x08000000 / 0x08040000 are hard-coded magic numbers, while bl_config.h already defines the memory map (APP_FLASH_BASE, BL_FLASH_BASE, FLASH end at 0x08040000). The literals here are not derived from those constants and can silently drift if the layout changes.
findings.impact: Maintenance hazard only; no current defect (256KB part end is correct for STM32WL55JC). If the layout macros change but these literals do not, the range guard would diverge from the real map.
findings.recommendation: Replace the literals with constants from bl_config.h (e.g. APP_FLASH_BASE for the low bound and a FLASH_END/0x08040000 macro for the high bound) so the guard tracks the canonical layout.

findings.description: MISRA-like nits: loop index declared as plain int (line 50) for a fixed 0..7 count (prefer unsigned); the 0x80000000 mask (line 51) lacks a U suffix (CRC32_INIT_VALUE and the polynomial use UL but this bare hex constant does not), and crc32_byte takes/returns plain uint32_t without const on inputs.
findings.impact: No functional impact on this 32-bit target, but inconsistent with the file's own UL convention and the project's stated MISRA-like discipline; bare 0x80000000 is int-typed and could surprise on a different width.
findings.recommendation: Use 0x80000000UL, an unsigned loop counter, and keep suffix conventions consistent across the file.

dead_code: Genuine orphan dead state: static bool crc_initialized (line 23) is written by bl_crc_init/bl_crc_deinit but never read — write-only, no behavioral effect. bl_crc_deinit (line 32) is exported but never called anywhere in the project and only mutates that dead flag, making it an effective no-op. bl_crc32_calculate is reachable only transitively (via bl_crc32_flash); the header also exports bl_crc32_accumulate/get which ARE called from bl_dfu.c, and bl_crc_init/reset from bl_main.c/bl_dfu.c, so those are live. No config-gated dead code (bootloader is a single build).
test_coverage: Inadequate. Tests/unit/test_crc32.c tests a copied-in private implementation, not the bl_crc.c symbols, so the actual shipped code (NULL/zero guards, accumulate state machine, bl_crc32_get/reset, bl_crc32_flash range+overflow guard) is uncovered. Concrete gaps to add: (1) chunked accumulate == single-shot equivalence; (2) bl_crc32_flash rejects out-of-range start and out-of-range start+length (the over-read finding); (3) NULL/zero-length return contract per function; (4) accumulate-over-padded-bytes == bl_crc32_flash-over-flash for a non-8-aligned final chunk (the DFU padding mismatch finding). Link the real bl_crc.c into the test target rather than re-pasting the algorithm.

role: DFU protocol command handler for the standalone bootloader: parses/executes PING, GET_INFO, ERASE, WRITE, READ, VERIFY, GET_STATUS, SET_HEADER, ABORT; owns the file-static dfu_context_t (session/CRC/verify state) consumed by the UART and SPI DFU drivers.
compiled_in: Bootloader is a separate firmware image built by its own Makefile (Bootloader/), independent of APP/BOARD/COMM. Lives at 0x08033000. Reachable in the sealed UW_DOPPLER deployment only via AT+BOOT -> DFU flag -> jump to bootloader. Not part of the main app link.

findings.location: bl_dfu.c:267-296 (bl_dfu_cmd_read); reachable via bl_main.c:403-422 UART 'AT+DFU=READ' and bl_main.c:484-495 SPI READ_REQ
findings.description: READ command performs NO session check and NO app-region restriction. It memcpy's directly from any address within the whole 256 KB flash window (bl_flash_read only validates address>=FLASH_BASE and end<=FLASH_BASE+256KB, see bl_flash.c:199-224). The Kineis credentials (ID/ADDR/SECKEY) live at FLASH_USER 0x0803B000 and the credential mirror at FLASH_PMLOG 0x08032800 - both inside that window and both readable via DFU READ.
findings.impact: A host with serial/SPI access to a bootloader-mode device can dump the Kineis secret key and radio credentials, and the entire bootloader image, with no DFU session required. For a sealed unit this is only reachable after AT+BOOT, but it is an unrestricted secret-exfiltration primitive that the WRITE path (which is app-region-bounded) deliberately avoids.
findings.recommendation: Restrict READ to the application region: reject if !bl_flash_addr_in_app(address) || !bl_flash_addr_in_app(address+read_len-1). If READ is only meant for write-back verification, that range is sufficient; never expose FLASH_USER / FLASH_PMLOG / bootloader.

findings.description: read_len is silently clamped to *response_len ('if (read_len > *response_len) read_len = *response_len;') instead of returning DFU_RSP_SIZE_ERROR. The host asked for N bytes and is told DFU_RSP_OK with fewer, with no length-mismatch signal beyond the returned response_len. In the UART path response is 512 B so clamping rarely bites, but in the SPI READ_REQ path read_buf is only BL_CHUNK_SIZE (248, bl_main.c:486) so any request >248 is truncated and reported as success.
findings.impact: A read-back verification host comparing the requested length against returned data could mis-handle the short read; at best a confusing protocol, at worst a verification that passes on truncated data. Not a memory-safety issue (clamp prevents overflow) but a silent-correctness defect.
findings.recommendation: Return DFU_RSP_SIZE_ERROR when the requested read_len exceeds *response_len rather than clamping, so the host learns its request did not fit.

findings.description: Inconsistent precondition checking: WRITE (line 199) and VERIFY (line 303) both guard on session_active, but READ has neither a session check nor any address-range guard (see also the high finding). The 'Validate' comment at line 281 only covers the length-vs-buffer clamp, giving a false sense that the address was validated.
findings.impact: Reinforces the unrestricted-read exposure and makes the handler's contract inconsistent and easy to mis-maintain.
findings.recommendation: Add a session/app-range precondition consistent with WRITE, and fix the misleading 'Validate' comment to say what is actually validated.

findings.description: SET_HEADER writes the app header at APP_HEADER_ADDR=0x08000200 (inside the first app page). When dfu_ctx.erase_done is true (normal flow: ERASE ran first), it SKIPS the per-page erase (line 382) and calls bl_flash_write directly. Flash NOR can only program 1->0; if SET_HEADER is ever issued twice in one session, or after WRITE already programmed bytes in page 0, the second program of non-erased cells will fail or corrupt. The function also never sets a session and does not require erase_done, so calling SET_HEADER first (erase_done=false) erases ONLY the header page (line 389) leaving the rest of page 0 (the vector table at 0x08000000) intact/uninitialized.
findings.impact: In the documented flow header writing is benign, but the 'erase just the header page' branch erases a 2 KB page that also contains the ISR vector table (0x08000000-0x080001FF). If SET_HEADER is used standalone before WRITE, it wipes the vector table region of an existing app without rewriting it - a path to a non-booting image. Low probability in the scripted flow, but it is an unsynchronized erase of a shared page.
findings.recommendation: Make SET_HEADER require an active erased session (session_active && erase_done), or have it erase/rewrite the whole first page atomically. At minimum document that page 0 holds the vector table and a partial erase there leaves the app unbootable.

findings.location: bl_dfu.h:32 total_size field; set nowhere, read nowhere
findings.description: dfu_context_t.total_size is never written and never read anywhere in the bootloader (grep: only the struct definition). It is a genuine orphan field, not config-gated.
findings.impact: None functional; dead state that suggests an intended 'expected total size' bound check on WRITE that was never implemented (so WRITE has no cumulative-size cap beyond per-chunk address bounds).
findings.recommendation: Either remove total_size, or wire it (GET_INFO/host could set it and WRITE could enforce received_size<=total_size). Note the per-chunk end-bound at bl_dfu.c:241 already prevents overrun past APP region, so the missing cap is not a safety bug, only unused state.

findings.location: bl_dfu.c:409 header_written field set; never read
findings.description: dfu_ctx.header_written is set to true in SET_HEADER but is never read by any consumer (not in bl_dfu_is_complete/can_jump, not in bl_spi_protocol_build_extended_status, grep-confirmed). Genuine orphan, not config-gated.
findings.impact: None; misleading because JUMP eligibility (can_jump) does NOT require a header to have been written - header presence is not part of the completeness criteria despite this flag existing.
findings.recommendation: Remove the field, or include header_written in the jump-readiness decision if a valid header is actually required to boot the new app.

findings.description: aligned_data is a function-static scratch buffer used to pad WRITE payloads. memcpy at line 231 copies the un-padded payload_len, then memset pads the tail; the leading bytes are always overwritten so there is no stale-data leak. However the buffer is function-static (not re-entrant) which is fine for the bootloader's single-threaded superloop but is an implicit invariant worth a comment. Also BL_CHUNK_SIZE+8 sizing relies on payload_len<=BL_CHUNK_SIZE (checked at 223) so aligned_len<=BL_CHUNK_SIZE rounded up <= BL_CHUNK_SIZE (248 is already %8==0) -> max 248 <= 256. Bound holds.
findings.impact: No defect; the +8 slack is sufficient because BL_CHUNK_SIZE is a multiple of 8. If BL_CHUNK_SIZE were ever changed to a non-multiple-of-8 the rounding could need up to +7, still within +8. Brittle on a future config change.
findings.recommendation: Add a _Static_assert((BL_CHUNK_SIZE % 8) == 0) near the buffer (or in bl_config.h) to lock the invariant the alignment math depends on.

findings.description: On the DFU_CMD_PING / GET_INFO / READ / GET_STATUS branches, *response_len is NOT reset before the sub-handler runs, so the handlers rely on the caller having pre-loaded *response_len with the buffer capacity (bl_main.c:340 and :470 do this). That contract is undocumented at the process_cmd level. For DFU_CMD_RESET/JUMP and the default branch *response_len is explicitly zeroed, creating an inconsistent pattern where some paths set it and some assume the caller did.
findings.impact: If a future caller forgets to initialize *response_len before calling for PING/INFO/READ/STATUS, the size guards (e.g. line 112, 139, 282, 340) read an uninitialized 'max length' and could under- or over-report. Currently safe because both callers initialize it.
findings.recommendation: Document in bl_dfu.h that *response_len is in/out (in=capacity) for response-producing commands, or defensively snapshot capacity at the top of process_cmd.

findings.location: bl_dfu.c whole file; Tests/unit has no bl_dfu coverage (grep of Tests/ finds no bl_dfu test)
findings.description: None of the pure-logic DFU handlers are unit-tested. The high-value testable logic that does not need real flash: WRITE alignment/padding math (bl_dfu.c:227-243) and its end-of-region bound check, the session/erase precondition gating, VERIFY CRC compare and verify_passed latching, can_jump/is_complete state logic, GET_INFO byte layout (must match the Zephyr 15-byte format), and the READ length clamp. bl_flash_* and bl_crc_* can be mocked as the project already mocks HAL_/MGR_.
findings.impact: Protocol-format and state-machine regressions (e.g. the GET_INFO 15-byte layout, or can_jump returning true without verify) would ship unnoticed; this is the firmware-update path for sealed units where a bad jump-gate could brick the field device.
findings.recommendation: Add Tests/unit/test_bl_dfu.c covering: WRITE rejects when no session; WRITE end-bound rejects a chunk straddling APP_FLASH_END; VERIFY sets/clears verify_passed and can_jump follows; GET_INFO emits exactly 15 bytes with correct LE app_start/max_size/page_size; READ clamp/range behavior (will also pin the fix for the high finding).

dead_code: Two genuine orphan fields in dfu_context_t: total_size (bl_dfu.h:32) is never written or read; header_written (set at bl_dfu.c:409) is never read. Neither is config-gated -- both are leftover/unwired state, not intentional. All 9 bl_dfu_cmd_* handlers and the bool query functions (is_complete/can_jump/session_active/get_context) are live: reached from bl_main.c UART handler (lines 433-449), SPI handler (lines 488,534-556), and bl_spi_protocol.c:236. No dead branches inside the switch (every dfu_cmd_t value handled; default returns INVALID_CMD). The BL_DEBUG snprintf block (bl_dfu.c:317-324) is compiled only when DEBUG=1 and must be stripped from sealed-deploy builds (it is, since prod builds DEBUG=0).
test_coverage: No unit tests exist for bl_dfu (Tests/unit has no bl_dfu file; grep confirms). The pure-logic parts ARE testable with mocked bl_flash_*/bl_crc_* (the framework already mocks HAL_/MGR_): WRITE alignment+padding+end-bound math, session/erase gating, VERIFY CRC latch, can_jump/is_complete, GET_INFO 15-byte layout, READ clamp/range. These are currently untested -- concrete gap on the field firmware-update path.

role: Bootloader flash primitives: unlock/lock, page erase, 64-bit aligned write+readback-verify, read, region predicates, and DFU-request flag access via RTC backup register/SRAM (flash-resident BL state is compiled out).
compiled_in: Bootloader image only (separate build at 0x08033000), independent of APP/BOARD/COMM. The BL_STATE_PERSIST_ENABLED block is compiled out in every configuration.

findings.description: bl_flash_read() accepts any address in [FLASH_BASE, FLASH_BASE+256KB), i.e. the ENTIRE flash including the bootloader (0x08033000) AND the Kineis credentials/FLASH_USER region (0x0803B000: ID/ADDR/SECKEY/RADIOCONF). The DFU READ command (bl_dfu.c:287) passes the attacker/host-supplied address straight through with no app-region restriction (unlike WRITE/ERASE which use bl_flash_addr_in_app). So the DFU READ command can dump the secret AES key and Kineis credentials over the UART/SPI wire.
findings.impact: Confidentiality breach on a sealed deployment: anyone with magnet+serial access (or the SPI bus) can read the Kineis secret key and device credentials via DFU READ. Read-only, so no brick — but the credentials are supposed to be write/erase protected; they are not read-protected here.
findings.recommendation: If DFU READ is meant only for app verification, bound it with bl_flash_addr_in_app(address) && bl_flash_addr_in_app(address+length-1) the same way WRITE is bounded, instead of the full-flash BL_FLASH_TOTAL_SIZE bound. If full-flash read is genuinely needed for diagnostics, gate the credential/bootloader pages behind an explicit allow and document the leak.

findings.description: Unbounded busy-wait: `while ((PWR->CR1 & PWR_CR1_DBP) == 0);` with no timeout. PWR is always clocked on STM32WL and DBP is a normal RW bit that sets immediately, so in practice this returns at once — but it is an unconditional infinite loop with no IWDG kick and no escape. Any silicon/voltage anomaly that prevents DBP latching hangs the bootloader forever, which on a sealed unit means a permanently bricked device with no recovery (bootloader is the last-resort recovery path).
findings.impact: Theoretical hang in the boot/DFU path of a sealed deployment. Low probability but unrecoverable (no watchdog visible in this function), and it sits on the critical DFU-flag-read path called at bl_main.c:217.
findings.recommendation: Add a bounded spin (loop counter, a few thousand iterations) and proceed/return on timeout; DBP polling failure should not be fatal because subsequent TAMP/SRAM reads either succeed or are harmlessly skipped.

findings.description: When length is not a multiple of 8, the final partial chunk is written as a full 64-bit doubleword (remaining bytes from src, rest padded 0xFF). This programs 8 bytes starting at current_addr even though fewer than 8 were requested, i.e. it writes up to 7 bytes PAST address+length. There is no check that address+length is still inside the app region (the per-doubleword guard only rejects the bootloader region, not FLASH_PMLOG/FLASH_USER). For the live caller this branch is unreachable because bl_dfu.c always pre-pads to an 8-multiple (aligned_len, bl_dfu.c:233-236) and bounds address+aligned_len-1 to the app region (bl_dfu.c:241), so remaining is always 0 here. It is a latent overrun if this function is ever reused with a non-8-multiple length near a region boundary.
findings.impact: No impact in the current build (dead branch for the only caller). Latent: a future caller passing a non-multiple-of-8 length whose end lands at 0x08031FF9..0x08031FFF would silently program into FLASH_PMLOG (credential CRC mirror @0x08032800 page) bytes beyond the requested data.
findings.recommendation: Either reject non-8-multiple lengths outright (the alignment contract is already documented in the header: 'length must be multiple of 8'), or bound the padded end address against the app region before the final program, mirroring the start-address bootloader guard.

findings.description: bl_flash_verify() does memcmp((void*)address, ...) with NO address-range validation — unlike bl_flash_read() which validates the range. A bad address would fault or compare garbage. Current callers (bl_dfu.c:253 and :405) pass app/header addresses already validated by bl_flash_addr_in_app/APP_HEADER_ADDR, so it is safe today, but the asymmetry with bl_flash_read is an inconsistency and a trap for future callers.
findings.impact: No current defect (callers pre-validate). Robustness/consistency gap.
findings.recommendation: Add the same FLASH_BASE/total-size (or app-region) bound used in bl_flash_read before the memcmp, or document that the caller must pre-validate.

findings.description: bl_flash_get_page computes (address - FLASH_BASE)/FLASH_PAGE_SIZE with no check that address >= FLASH_BASE; an address below FLASH_BASE underflows to a huge page number. Only caller is bl_flash_erase_page (line 60), which already validates page alignment and the bootloader region but NOT address >= FLASH_BASE. In the live path bl_flash_erase_app passes APP_FLASH_BASE..0x08031FFF and the DFU header-erase passes APP_HEADER_ADDR, all >= FLASH_BASE, so the underflow is unreachable today. HAL_FLASHEx_Erase would also reject an out-of-range page via its own IS_FLASH_PAGE assert.
findings.impact: No current defect; latent if a sub-FLASH_BASE address ever reaches erase_page.
findings.recommendation: Add an `address >= FLASH_BASE` (or in-flash-range) guard in bl_flash_erase_page before computing the page, returning BL_FLASH_ADDR_ERROR.

findings.description: Return value of bl_flash_lock() is ignored at every call site (lines 108, 172, 194, and 298 in dead code). bl_flash_lock can return BL_FLASH_ERROR if HAL_FLASH_Lock fails; a failure to re-lock leaves flash unlocked (a write-protection robustness concern) but is silently dropped. Also bl_flash_erase_app() calls bl_flash_unlock() at line 93 while each underlying bl_flash_erase_page does its own erase under that single unlock — fine — but a stray failure to re-lock is unreported.
findings.impact: Minor: flash could remain unlocked after a failed lock with no signal. Low risk (HAL_FLASH_Lock effectively always succeeds), but on a brick-sensitive target an unlocked flash window is undesirable.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, propagate or log the lock failure; or accept it and add a brief comment that lock-failure is non-actionable.

findings.description: Layering nit: bl_flash_erase_app unlocks once then calls bl_flash_erase_page repeatedly (each only does HAL erase, no nested unlock) — correct. But bl_flash_write also unlocks (line 160) and then calls bl_flash_write_doubleword which programs directly (no nested unlock) — also correct. The two public entry points each manage their own unlock/lock; bl_flash_erase_page and bl_flash_write_doubleword assume flash is already unlocked by the caller but are also public API (header lines 64,95) with no unlock of their own. A caller invoking bl_flash_erase_page() or bl_flash_write_doubleword() directly (not via erase_app/write) would operate on LOCKED flash and HAL would return an error. No current caller does this, but the contract (who unlocks) is undocumented and inconsistent across the public surface.
findings.impact: No defect today. Confusing/inconsistent public contract; easy to misuse later.
findings.recommendation: Document in the header that bl_flash_erase_page/bl_flash_write_doubleword require the caller to have unlocked flash, or make them self-contained.

findings.description: Confirmed intentional dead code (config-gated): bl_flash_read_bl_state, bl_flash_write_bl_state, bl_flash_set_dfu_request are compiled out via BL_STATE_PERSIST_ENABLED==0. Their BL_STATE_FLASH_ADDR (0x0803B000) aliases FLASH_USER page0 = the Kineis credentials; bl_flash_write_bl_state would erase that page. The _Static_assert(BL_STATE_FLASH_ADDR != FLASH_USER_START) at bl_config.h:168 fails the build on any naive re-enable. This matches commit 15d349d / the flash-safety-guards commit and the MEMORY note (brick_hunt_seal). State: SAFE as-is, well-commented. Only nit: the _Static_assert is itself inside #if BL_STATE_PERSIST_ENABLED so it does not fire in the current (disabled) build — which is the intended behavior, but it means the guard is purely a re-enable tripwire, not an always-on invariant.
findings.impact: None currently (dead code, cannot run, cannot erase credentials).
findings.recommendation: No action needed. Optionally keep an always-compiled _Static_assert variant that asserts the relocation requirement unconditionally for extra safety, but current guard is acceptable.

findings.location: Bootloader/Src/bl_flash.c (entire file); Tests/unit has zero references to bl_flash
findings.description: No unit tests exist for any bl_flash logic (grep of Tests/ for 'bl_flash' = no matches). The pure-logic, HW-independent parts are eminently testable with a flash-memory mock: bl_flash_get_page arithmetic, bl_flash_erase_app page-count (the load-bearing 100-page/200KB bound that must NOT touch FLASH_PMLOG @0x08032000 — a regression here directly bricks credential recovery), bl_flash_addr_in_app / bl_flash_addr_in_bootloader boundary inclusivity, bl_flash_read overflow/range checks (lines 206-218), and the write chunking/remainder-padding loop. This is the most brick-relevant arithmetic in the bootloader and is entirely uncovered.
findings.impact: A future edit to APP_FLASH_SIZE, the page-count formula, or the region predicates could silently extend erase/write into FLASH_PMLOG (cred CRC mirror) or FLASH_USER (creds) with no test catching it — exactly the brick class the flash-safety-guards commit was defending against.
findings.recommendation: Add Tests/unit cases for: bl_flash_erase_app computes 100 pages and the last erased page is 0x08031800 (never 0x08032000+); bl_flash_get_page boundary values; addr_in_app/addr_in_bootloader at region edges; bl_flash_read rejects address<FLASH_BASE, integer overflow (length>UINT32_MAX-address), and end>256KB; write loop handles 8-multiple and (if kept) non-multiple lengths. Mock HAL_FLASH_* per the project test framework.

dead_code: Intentional config-gated dead code: bl_flash_read_bl_state / bl_flash_write_bl_state / bl_flash_set_dfu_request (lines 245-332) are compiled out by BL_STATE_PERSIST_ENABLED==0 (bl_config.h:166). They are NOT orphans — they are a deliberately disabled flash-resident-state feature whose target page aliases the Kineis credentials; left in source as documented, build-tripwired by a _Static_assert. Reachable-but-effectively-unused branch: the trailing-remainder padding branch in bl_flash_write (lines 181-191) is never taken by the sole caller (bl_dfu always pre-pads to an 8-multiple), so it is dead for the live build though not config-gated. Everything else (init, unlock, lock, erase_page, erase_pages, erase_app, write_doubleword, write, read, verify, addr_in_app, addr_in_bootloader, get_page, is_dfu_requested, clear_dfu_request, enable_backup_access_bl) is live and reachable from bl_dfu.c/bl_main.c.
test_coverage: Not covered. Tests/unit has zero references to bl_flash (confirmed by grep). The HW-independent, brick-critical logic is untested: erase_app page-count/200KB bound (must stop before FLASH_PMLOG @0x08032000), get_page arithmetic, addr_in_app/addr_in_bootloader boundaries, and bl_flash_read range/overflow checks. These are exactly the arithmetic paths that, if regressed, erase or read the Kineis credentials. Recommend mocked-HAL unit tests as detailed in the test-gap finding.

role: Bootloader entry point + state machine: HW/clock init, DFU-flag detection, UART/SPI protocol detection, DFU command dispatch (UART AT+DFU= and SPI A+), app header/CRC validation, and the validated jump-to-app. Built as a standalone program at 0x08033000.
compiled_in: Built as a SEPARATE program via Bootloader/Makefile, independent of the app's APP/BOARD/COMM matrix. Flags: PROTOCOL (UART|SPI -> BL_PROTOCOL_UART/SPI), DEBUG (0/1 -> BL_DEBUG/BL_DBG), BL_LED (0/1), BL_UART_BAUD (-> BL_UART_BAUDRATE). For the sealed deployment the top Makefile `bootloader` target builds it with PROTOCOL=UART, BL_UART_BAUD=115200, BL_LED=1, DEBUG=0. So in the deployed image: BL_LED block IS compiled, BL_DBG is a no-op, baud=115200 (BRR_115200 path), and the SPI DFU path is still compiled in (PROTOCOL only flips the default baud + BL_PROTOCOL_UART define, it does NOT remove SPI).

findings.description: bl_state_error() unconditionally routes to BL_STATE_DFU_UART when detected_protocol != BL_PROTO_SPI, including when detected_protocol == BL_PROTO_NONE. That NONE case is reachable: cold boot with NO DFU flag -> bl_state_init -> BL_STATE_CHECK_APP -> bl_check_app_valid()==true -> BL_STATE_JUMP_APP -> bl_jump_to_app(). If the jump's own SP/entry validation (617-624) fails and returns (it uses a DIFFERENT, stricter check than bl_check_app_valid: bl_check_app_valid reads SP/entry from the HEADER's app_start_addr-derived fallback only when header invalid, while jump reads SP/entry from header->app_start_addr when header magic is valid — the two can disagree), line 186 sets current_state=BL_STATE_ERROR with detected_protocol still BL_PROTO_NONE. bl_state_error then sets BL_STATE_DFU_UART, but neither bl_uart_init() nor bl_uart_start_rx() was ever called on this path (no DETECT_PROTOCOL was run). bl_state_dfu_uart() then calls bl_uart_process() on an uninitialized UART.
findings.impact: On a unit whose app header is present/valid but whose vector-table SP/entry words fail jump validation, the bootloader lands in a UART-DFU state with the UART peripheral never initialized — it will not service AT+DFU= commands and provides no recovery, i.e. an effectively bricked unit with no field input (sealed). Low probability but a genuine no-recovery hang path.
findings.recommendation: In bl_state_error(), when detected_protocol == BL_PROTO_NONE, run protocol detection (set state to BL_STATE_DETECT_PROTOCOL) instead of jumping straight to DFU_UART; or have bl_state_error() lazily call bl_uart_init()/bl_uart_start_rx() before entering DFU_UART. Also make bl_check_app_valid() and bl_jump_to_app() share one validation routine so they cannot disagree.

findings.description: Off-by-one in the entry-point upper bound: `app_entry > (APP_FLASH_BASE + APP_FLASH_SIZE)` permits app_entry == APP_FLASH_BASE + APP_FLASH_SIZE (== 0x08032000), which is the FIRST byte of FLASH_PMLOG, i.e. OUTSIDE the app code region (APP_FLASH_END is 0x08031FFF per bl_config.h:142). The comparison should be `>=`. bl_validate_app_header() at 709/713 uses the correct exclusive bounds (app_start_addr==APP_FLASH_BASE and app_size<=APP_MAX_SIZE), so this is only the fallback/jump path.
findings.impact: An entry point pointing exactly at 0x08032000 (FLASH_PMLOG / credential-mirror region) would pass the gate and be jumped to. Extremely narrow window (one 32-bit-aligned address, Thumb bit must be set so 0x08032001) and requires a malformed/corrupt vector table, so low practical risk, but it is a validation-gate off-by-one in a brick-relevant path.
findings.recommendation: Use `>=`: `if (app_entry < APP_FLASH_BASE || app_entry >= (APP_FLASH_BASE + APP_FLASH_SIZE)) return;` in both bl_jump_to_app (622) and bl_check_app_valid (688). Consider also rejecting entry points with bit0 clear (non-Thumb).

findings.description: bl_jump_to_app touches SPI1->CR1, SPI1->SR and SPI1->DR (632-639) unconditionally, but the SPI1 peripheral bus clock is enabled ONLY inside bl_spi_init() (bl_spi.c:79). On the forced-UART / STANDALONE deployment path, bl_spi_init() is never called (bl_state_detect_protocol forced-UART branch at 248-255 inits only UART), so at JUMP time SPI1 is clock-gated. Reads/writes to a clock-gated APB peripheral on STM32WL are silently ignored (no bus fault on Cortex-M4), so the `while ((SPI1->SR & SPI_SR_RXNE) ...)` reads 0 and exits immediately — functionally harmless today, but it relies on implementation-defined 'access-to-disabled-peripheral is ignored' behavior and is fragile.
findings.impact: No fault today, but a latent dependency on disabled-peripheral-access semantics. If the drain loop ever depended on a real SPI1->SR bit it would misbehave. The __HAL_RCC_SPI1_FORCE_RESET/RELEASE (641-643) are RCC ops and remain safe.
findings.recommendation: Guard the SPI1 register drain (632-639) behind a check that SPI was actually initialized (e.g. only when detected_protocol==BL_PROTO_SPI, or test RCC->APB2ENR SPI1EN), or enable the SPI1 clock briefly before touching its registers.

findings.description: current_state and detected_protocol are plain `static` (non-volatile) and are read/written from the main loop only; no ISR writes them (SysTick_Handler only calls HAL_IncTick). So no race today. However bl_set_state()/bl_get_state() are exported in bl_main.h as public API; if any IRQ handler in another TU ever called bl_set_state, the non-volatile state variable would be a problem. early_dfu_flag_detected and early_proto_flag are correctly volatile but are also only touched from main context.
findings.impact: No current defect (single-threaded cooperative loop). Flagged as a latent invariant: the state var is not volatile despite a public setter.
findings.recommendation: Document that bl_set_state must never be called from ISR context, or mark current_state volatile if that contract cannot be guaranteed. No change required for the current code.

findings.location: bl_main.c:346-423 (UART command parse, strncmp prefix matching)
findings.description: Command dispatch uses fixed-length strncmp prefixes that can mis-match by prefix overlap. 'AT+DFU=READ' (11 chars, line 403) is tested AFTER 'AT+DFU=RESET' (12, line 397), 'AT+DFU=WRITE' (line 364) and 'AT+DFU=VERIFY' (line 352) — fine because longer/distinct prefixes are tested first. But the parser does not verify the command terminator: e.g. 'AT+DFU=PINGXYZ' matches DFU_CMD_PING (strncmp 11). Harmless for action commands, but for WRITE/READ/VERIFY the trailing-arg parsing relies on strtoul tolerance. cmd_buffer is also assumed NUL-terminated by bl_uart_get_command — strncmp/strtoul depend on that NUL being within BL_CMD_BUFFER_SIZE; this is guaranteed by the uart layer but is an implicit cross-module contract.
findings.impact: No overflow (strncmp is length-bounded, strtoul stops at first non-hex). Worst case is a slightly permissive command grammar. Low risk.
findings.recommendation: Optional: after the prefix match, check the next char is ',' , '\0', '\r' or '\n' to reject 'AT+DFU=PINGxyz'. Confirm bl_uart_get_command always NUL-terminates within max_len (it is passed sizeof(cmd_buffer)).

findings.description: early_debug_update_baudrate() toggles UE off/on and re-selects the LPUART1 clock source but does NOT rewrite LPUART1->BRR. It is called from bl_init() (113) AFTER early_debug_init() (924, from main) already set BRR=EARLY_DEBUG_BRR. So the function name implies a baud change but it never changes the baud register — it only re-asserts the clock source and waits for TEACK. The name is misleading (comment-rot risk): nothing updates the baudrate here. Also early_debug_init() is static and only called once from main(); its TEACK/HSI fallbacks silently `return` on timeout leaving UART half-configured, but since DEBUG=0 in deployment the only output via this path is the banner + HardFault message.
findings.impact: No functional bug. Misleading name/comment; a maintainer may assume calling it re-derives BRR for a new clock and be surprised. Cosmetic.
findings.recommendation: Rename to early_debug_reassert_clock() or actually recompute/write BRR inside it. No behavioral change needed for deployment.

findings.description: main() enables RCC_APB1ENR1_RTCAPBEN and sets PWR_CR1_DBP (backup-domain write protection disabled) to read/clear TAMP_BKP0R, and never re-disables DBP nor clears RTCAPBEN before jumping to the app. The app re-runs its own SystemClock/PWR init from reset (the app is entered via NVIC_SystemReset on the RESET/JUMP commands, not a direct call in the normal DFU finish — though BL_STATE_JUMP_APP does a direct bl_jump_to_app()). On the direct-jump path the app inherits DBP=1 and RTCAPBEN=1.
findings.impact: Minor: backup-domain write protection remains disabled across a direct jump until the app reconfigures PWR. For a security/robustness posture the backup registers are writable by stray code until app init. Power impact negligible. The app's own init normally re-establishes this.
findings.recommendation: Optionally clear PWR_CR1_DBP after reading/clearing TAMP_BKP0R (947) since the bootloader no longer needs backup-domain write access. Low priority.

findings.description: No unit test exercises any bl_main.c logic. Tests/unit has test_crc32.c (CRC algorithm only) and test_crash_forensics.c (app-side, not bootloader); test_boot_loop_*.c are the APP boot-loop manager, not this file. The pure-logic, HW-independent validation gates here (header magic/version/addr/size bounds, SP-in-RAM and entry-in-flash range checks, the off-by-one in finding above) are exactly the kind of code that should be unit-testable with a mocked flash/header.
findings.impact: The brick-relevant validation gates (which decide whether to jump to potentially-bad code) have zero automated coverage, so the off-by-one at 622/688 and the protocol==NONE error path went uncaught.
findings.recommendation: Add Tests/unit/test_bl_app_validate.c mocking bl_get_app_header()/flash to cover: valid header+CRC, bad magic, app_size==0, app_size>APP_MAX_SIZE, app_start!=APP_FLASH_BASE, SP just below SRAM_BASE / just above SRAM_END, entry==APP_FLASH_BASE+APP_FLASH_SIZE boundary (catches the off-by-one), and entry just below APP_FLASH_BASE.

dead_code: Config-gated (intentional, NOT orphans): (1) The entire BL_LED block (47-101, 119-121, 155-157, 436-442, 582-584, 627-629) is gated on -DBL_LED; in the sealed STANDALONE build BL_LED=1 so it IS live. (2) BL_DBG(...) calls (105-114, 282, 291, 300, 313, 569, 755-789, 951-953) compile to ((void)0) when DEBUG=0 (deployment) — early_debug_print() direct calls (220, 240, 249, etc., 925, 929) are always live. (3) The BRR_9600 path (808-812) is dead when BL_UART_BAUDRATE!=9600; deployment uses 115200 so EARLY_DEBUG_BRR=BRR_115200. (4) The SPI DFU path (bl_state_dfu_spi, forced-SPI branch) is compiled in even for PROTOCOL=UART but is unreachable in the STANDALONE deployment because the app there only ever forces UART (early_proto_flag never == DFU_PROTO_SPI) — config/data-gated, not an orphan. Genuine never-taken in practice: bl_state_detect_protocol legacy auto-detect block (257-326) is only reached when early_proto_flag==DFU_PROTO_NONE (auto), which the production app never sets for STANDALONE (it forces UART) — reachable only via the cold-boot-invalid-app path. No truly orphan (no-caller) functions found: all static helpers are referenced; all exported bl_* functions are part of the public API used by main()/state machine.
test_coverage: No unit test covers bl_main.c. Tests/unit/{test_crc32.c, test_crash_forensics.c, test_boot_loop_crc.c, test_boot_loop_time.c} are CRC-algorithm and APP-side boot-loop tests, none reference bl_main symbols (bl_check_app_valid, bl_validate_app_header, bl_jump_to_app, app_header_t). GAP: the HW-independent validation gates (header magic/version/addr/size, SP/entry range checks incl. the 622/688 off-by-one) and the bl_state_error protocol==NONE routing are unit-testable with mocked flash/header and currently untested. The HW glue (bl_hw_init clock setup, early_debug LPUART bit-banging, SPI1 teardown) is not unit-testable.

role: Bootloader DFU SPI1 slave driver (polling, baremetal): GPIO/peripheral init, raw 0xAA-idle transaction RX/TX over SPI1, frame validation, command/payload extraction, multi-transaction WRITE_REQ->WRITE_DATA and READ_REQ->READ_DATA state, response framing handoff to the A+ protocol layer.
compiled_in: all bootloader builds (separate image). bl_spi.c is in Makefile SOURCES unconditionally and USE_SPI_DRIVER is always defined; PROTOCOL=UART vs SPI only changes the default DFU baud and BL_PROTOCOL_SPI define, not whether this file links. SPI DFU path is reachable at runtime whenever a SPI master drives the bootloader (forced via early_proto_flag==DFU_PROTO_SPI, or auto-detect). Not part of the application image.

findings.description: When a valid A+ frame carries data_len in 249..255 (uint8_t LEN allows up to 255, but payload_buffer is BL_CHUNK_SIZE=248), the guard `if (payload_len > 0 && payload_len <= BL_CHUNK_SIZE)` SKIPS the memcpy into payload_buffer, yet payload_len is still set to the oversized value (line 444 `payload_len = request->data_len`). cmd_ready becomes true. The non-WRITE_DATA branch of bl_spi_get_payload (line 485) then does `len = (payload_len < max_len) ? payload_len : max_len; memcpy(buffer, payload_buffer, len)` and copies up to 248 bytes of STALE payload_buffer contents (leftover from a previous command) to the caller as if it were this command's payload. No error is returned; the bootloader silently acts on stale data.
findings.impact: A malformed/oversized SPI frame (or a host bug producing LEN 249..255) makes a DFU command operate on stale payload bytes instead of being rejected. For SET_HEADER / VERIFY / ERASE-with-args this can write a wrong app header or wrong CRC/address into flash silently. On a sealed unit the bootloader is the only field-recovery path, so a corrupt update that still reports OK is a brick risk.
findings.recommendation: Reject the frame when payload_len > BL_CHUNK_SIZE: send DFU_RSP_SIZE_ERROR (or BL_PROT error), call bl_spi_start_rx() and return false, instead of proceeding with cmd_ready=true. Do not leave payload_len set when the copy was skipped.

findings.description: Loop-count timeouts use `--loop_timeout > 0` with loop_timeout = SystemCoreClock/16. The comment claims '~200ms at 32 MHz', but the bound is purely iteration-count based and varies with actual CPU clock, optimization level, and whether the FIFO feeds. If SystemCoreClock is higher (or the loop body is faster than assumed) the real timeout differs significantly from the documented 200ms. bl_spi_wait_tx_done uses a HAL_GetTick 500ms cap which is fine, but the two tight loops (poll_rx, handle_tx_poll) have no wall-clock backstop at all once NSS has gone low.
findings.impact: If a SPI master asserts NSS low and then stalls the clock (or glitches), the slave spins in the tight loop for an unpredictable duration. Not an infinite hang (decrementing counter terminates), but the worst-case duration is not the stated 200ms and is clock-dependent; on a faster clock the transfer window could be too short and silently truncate a legitimate transaction.
findings.recommendation: Add a HAL_GetTick()-based wall-clock backstop checked every N iterations (cheap), or derive loop_timeout from a measured cycles-per-iteration constant with a _Static_assert/comment tying it to SystemCoreClock. At minimum fix the comment to not assert a fixed 200ms that the code does not guarantee.

findings.description: Genuine orphans: these public functions have no caller anywhere in the bootloader (verified across bl_main.c, bl_dfu.c, bl_spi_protocol.c; they appear in bootloader.map only as standalone .text symbols with no referrers). bl_spi_irq_handler is an empty stub ('Not used in polling mode'). bl_spi_read/bl_spi_read_byte read rx_buffer[0..] independent of the command-parsing path. They are not config-gated — they are leftover API surface from a prior DMA/interrupt design.
findings.impact: Code bloat in a flash-constrained bootloader region and confusing API surface. bl_spi_read_byte/bl_spi_read returning raw rx_buffer could be misused later (they bypass poll-frame filtering and protocol parsing). No current runtime impact.
findings.recommendation: Remove the unused functions (and their header decls) or, if kept as intentional public API, mark with a comment that they are currently unused. At minimum drop the empty bl_spi_irq_handler.

findings.description: rx_count, rx_complete, cmd_ready, spi_state are declared `volatile` (and the file ships an empty bl_spi_irq_handler) implying an ISR/main shared-data design, but the driver is pure polling from a single baremetal context — there is no SPI ISR enabled. The volatile qualifiers are therefore unnecessary and only pessimize codegen. Conversely, payload_buffer/payload_len/current_cmd/pending_* are NOT volatile, so the volatile set is inconsistent and not actually protecting any cross-context invariant.
findings.impact: No correctness bug today (single-context polling). Misleading: suggests ISR safety that does not exist; if someone later wires the IRQ they will assume these are synchronized when no critical sections exist.
findings.recommendation: Drop volatile (single-context polling) OR document that it is retained intentionally; if the IRQ path is ever enabled, add proper critical sections rather than relying on volatile.

findings.description: Several busy-waits `while (!(SPI1->SR & SPI_SR_TXE));` (lines 201, 576) have NO timeout. In bl_spi_start_polling_rx (line 201) and bl_spi_send_response prefill (line 576), if TXE never asserts (peripheral wedged after an abort/reset race) the loop hangs forever. SPI was just FORCE_RESET/enabled so TXE should be set, but there is no guaranteed backstop.
findings.impact: Theoretical permanent hang of the bootloader if SPI1 TXE never sets (e.g., peripheral left in a bad state by a prior aborted transaction). In the sealed-deploy recovery path a hung bootloader with no watchdog kick means a dead unit until power-cycle (and bl_main's watchdog handling, if any, would not run).
findings.recommendation: Bound these TXE waits with a small loop-count or HAL_GetTick timeout like the other loops, and bail to BL_SPI_STATE_IDLE on expiry.

findings.description: bl_spi_send_response legacy branch (else, mode != A_PLUS) builds a raw status+data frame manually instead of calling bl_spi_protocol_build_legacy_response() which exists for exactly this. Line 526 computes `BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE - 1` and compares against uint16_t data_len; the mixed signed/unsigned int arithmetic is fine here (512-1 fits), but duplicating the framing logic risks divergence from the protocol layer. Also this branch is taken when mode==BL_PROT_MODE_UNKNOWN (e.g. if send_response were ever called before any frame parsed), producing a 16-byte legacy-padded frame a host in A+ mode would not expect.
findings.impact: Maintenance hazard / minor protocol-mismatch risk. In practice mode is always set by bl_spi_protocol_process before any send_response in the live path, so low severity.
findings.recommendation: Call bl_spi_protocol_build_legacy_response() to avoid duplicated framing, and assert/handle mode==UNKNOWN explicitly.

findings.description: Pin map comment vs MEMORY/BSP: SPI1 uses PA1(SCK), PA15(NSS), PB4(MISO), PB5(MOSI). On SMD_STDALONE these same pins (PA1/PB4/PB5) are the application's RGB LED lines (RED/GREEN/BLUE per BSP_LED_wiring memory). This is the documented intentional pin overlap (bootloader has no LED; app reuses the bus pins), so it is correct here, but it means while the bootloader holds SPI1 active these pins are driven as AF push-pull, not LED outputs. Worth flagging only so a future reviewer does not 'fix' a perceived conflict.
findings.impact: None — intentional shared-pin design. Noted for cross-board awareness.
findings.recommendation: No action; the existing comment block could add one line noting the app-LED overlap to prevent accidental edits.

findings.description: Frame validation is duplicated and uses magic numbers: bl_spi_has_data() requires `bytes >= 5 && rx_buffer[0]==BL_SPI_IDLE_PATTERN`, while is_poll_frame() checks the first 4 bytes against IDLE_PATTERN and returns true for len<5. The '5' and the 0xAA-vs-magic-request overload (BL_SPI_IDLE_PATTERN == BL_SPI_MAGIC_REQUEST == 0xAA) make the poll-vs-command discrimination fragile and hard to follow. A real A+ command frame legitimately starts with 0xAA magic, so the rx_buffer[0]==IDLE check at line 340 is really 'starts with magic', not 'is idle'.
findings.impact: No direct defect, but the dual meaning of 0xAA (idle pad AND A+ request magic) is a latent trap: a genuinely empty/idle transaction and a real A+ frame both begin with 0xAA and are distinguished only downstream by is_poll_frame()/protocol_process.
findings.recommendation: Use the named BL_SPI_FRAME_MIN_SIZE (=5) constant instead of literal 5, and add a comment that 0xAA doubles as idle pad and A+ magic so the first-byte test is intentionally permissive.

dead_code: Genuine orphans (no caller in bootloader, confirmed via grep over bl_main.c/bl_dfu.c/bl_spi_protocol.c and bootloader.map symbol refs): bl_spi_rx_available (354), bl_spi_read (359), bl_spi_read_byte (366), bl_spi_prepare_tx (373), bl_spi_flush_rx (381), bl_spi_irq_handler (605, empty stub). These are NOT config-gated — leftover public API from a prior DMA/IRQ design. spi_debug_hex8 (58) is config-gated behind BL_DEBUG (live only when DEBUG=1). All other functions (init, deinit, start/stop_rx, has_data, process, get_command, get_payload, send_response, store/get/has_read_data, wait_tx_done) are live via bl_state_dfu_spi/bl_state_detect_protocol in bl_main.c.
test_coverage: Partial. Tests/unit/test_spi_protocol.c covers the A+ framing/CRC layer (bl_spi_protocol.c), NOT this driver. The pure-logic functions in bl_spi.c that SHOULD have unit tests but do not: (1) bl_spi_process payload extraction / WRITE_REQ addr+len decode (lines 451-455) and the WRITE_DATA not-ready rejection (458-464); (2) the data_len 249..255 oversize handling (the high-sev stale-payload bug above) — a direct unit test feeding data_len>BL_CHUNK_SIZE would catch it; (3) bl_spi_get_payload WRITE_DATA address-prepend and the `max_len < 4+payload_len` bound (478-483); (4) is_poll_frame discrimination. The polling RX/TX FIFO loops are HW glue (need SPI1 register mocks) and are reasonably n/a for unit tests, but the parsing/state logic is mockable and currently untested.

role: A+ framing layer for the bootloader's SPI DFU path: magic-byte frame parse, CRC-8, request/response build, legacy fallback, op-state + extended-status accessors.
compiled_in: all (bootloader is a separate image, always built; SPI vs UART is auto-detected at runtime in bl_main.c, so this file is LIVE in the sealed UW_DOPPLER/SMD_STDALONE/UART deployment too — the app's COMM=UART flag does not gate the bootloader).

findings.description: The unit test 'test_spi_protocol.c' does NOT include or link bl_spi_protocol.c. It tests local mock reimplementations (get_cmd_info, format_response, parse_write_req_frame, detector_*) that duplicate the logic with different code. The real functions bl_spi_protocol_process, bl_spi_protocol_crc8, bl_spi_protocol_build_response, bl_spi_protocol_build_legacy_response, bl_spi_protocol_build_extended_status have ZERO direct test coverage (grep for the real symbol names across Tests/ returns nothing).
findings.impact: The actual frame parser that runs in a sealed-unit bootloader during a field firmware update is unverified. A regression in CRC-8, the expected_len bounds check (line 94), the poll-frame guard (lines 79-81), or the data_len memcpy (line 99) would pass CI green. A malformed frame that the real parser mishandles could desync or hang an OTA update on a sealed device.
findings.recommendation: Add a unit suite that #includes the real bl_spi_protocol.c (with mocked bl_dfu_get_context/bl_get_state) and feeds it crafted byte buffers: short frame, length<MIN, data_len=255 boundary, CRC pass/fail, poll frame, legacy cmd, magic-byte-but-truncated, and a build_response/crc8 known-answer vector.

findings.description: seq_error_count is incremented (line 121) but never read anywhere — it is not exposed in bl_spi_protocol_build_extended_status (which only copies crc_error_count, line 255) and no caller reads it. It is a write-only counter. More importantly, a sequence mismatch only bumps the counter; the frame is still parsed and processed (no return false, no rejection). The A+ protocol therefore provides no replay/duplicate/out-of-order protection — sequence numbers are decorative.
findings.impact: If the SPI host re-sends a stale frame (e.g. retransmit after a missed response) the bootloader will re-execute it. For DFU that means a duplicated WRITE_DATA could re-apply at a stale address, or a re-sent JUMP/RESET could fire unexpectedly. Low probability (host-driven, point-to-point), but on a sealed unit any OTA corruption is unrecoverable.
findings.recommendation: Either act on the sequence check (reject/ignore a frame whose seq != expected and != 0, returning a SEQ_ERROR status) or remove the counter and the dead branch entirely and document that sequence is echo-only. If keeping it for diagnostics, also surface seq_error_count in the extended status so it is at least observable.

findings.description: bl_spi_protocol_build_response and bl_spi_protocol_build_legacy_response write into tx_buf with no buffer-length parameter and no bounds check. They blindly write 4 + data_len + 1 bytes then pad to 16. data_len is a uint8_t (max 255), so worst case is 260 bytes written. The only current caller (bl_spi.c:519) passes tx_buffer[BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE=512] and clamps data_len to 255, so it is safe today — but the API contract is unguarded.
findings.impact: Latent landmine: any future caller (or a refactor of BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE) that passes a buffer < 260 bytes silently overflows a static buffer in the bootloader. In the sealed bootloader an overflow corrupts adjacent statics and can brick an in-progress update.
findings.recommendation: Add a max-len parameter (or a compile-time _Static_assert(BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE >= BL_SPI_FRAME_HEADER_SIZE + BL_SPI_FRAME_MAX_DATA + BL_SPI_FRAME_CRC_SIZE) co-located with the builder) and clamp/return-0 on overflow. At minimum document the required minimum tx_buf size in the header (currently undocumented).

findings.description: Magic number 16 hardcoded as the minimum padded frame length in both builders ('while (index < 16)'). The same '16' appears independently in bl_spi.c:532-534. There is no named constant; BL_SPI_FRAME_MIN_SIZE is 5, so 16 is an unrelated SPI-minimum-transfer constant that is not defined anywhere.
findings.impact: If the SPI minimum transfer size assumption changes, three independent literals must be found and updated; mismatch would produce short responses the host mis-frames.
findings.recommendation: Define e.g. BL_SPI_MIN_RESPONSE_SIZE 16 in bl_spi_protocol.h and use it in both builders and in bl_spi.c.

findings.description: The 'else if (first_byte == 0xFF || first_byte == 0x00) return false;' branch is functionally identical to the final 'else return false;'. The explicit 0xFF/0x00 test produces no distinct behavior — it is redundant. (It may have been intended to distinguish idle/bus-float bytes for logging, but there is no log and no different return.)
findings.impact: None functionally; minor confusion / dead branch. Reviewer may assume 0xFF/0x00 are handled specially when they are not.
findings.recommendation: Collapse into the final else, or add the intended distinct handling (e.g. a debug counter for bus-idle bytes) if that was the goal.

findings.description: crc_offset (line 104) and crc_len (line 107) are computed from the identical expression 'BL_SPI_FRAME_HEADER_SIZE + protocol_ctx.request.data_len'. Two separate locals hold the same value; redundant computation and slight cognitive overhead (reader must verify they are equal).
findings.impact: None; correctness is fine (crc is computed over header+data, and the received crc sits immediately after at the same offset). Pure redundancy.
findings.recommendation: Use a single local 'uint16_t crc_pos = BL_SPI_FRAME_HEADER_SIZE + request.data_len;' for both the crc8 length and the received-crc index.

findings.description: Comment 'data_len is uint8_t so max 255, which equals BL_SPI_FRAME_MAX_DATA' is correct and load-bearing (it is the implicit guard that prevents the line-99 memcpy from overflowing request.data[255]). The safety relies entirely on data_len being uint8_t and request.data being exactly BL_SPI_FRAME_MAX_DATA. There is no _Static_assert enforcing data[] size == 255, so a future widening of data_len to uint16_t or a shrink of data[] would break the invariant silently.
findings.impact: Currently safe. The invariant is comment-only, not compiler-enforced — a fragile bounds guarantee in a sealed-unit code path.
findings.recommendation: Add _Static_assert(sizeof(((bl_spi_request_t*)0)->data) >= 255) (or == BL_SPI_FRAME_MAX_DATA) near the memcpy or in the header to make the bound compiler-checked.

dead_code: No genuine orphan functions: all 16 exported functions are reachable. Callers — init/process/get_request/get_ctx/build_response from bl_spi.c; set_op_state from bl_main.c:527-592; build_extended_status from bl_dfu.c:359; is_valid_dfu_cmd/crc8 internally. Confirmed-unused exports that ARE in the public header but have NO caller: bl_spi_protocol_reset (defined :21, declared :183, zero callers found), bl_spi_protocol_is_legacy (:153, zero callers — consumers read prot_ctx->mode directly at bl_spi.c:436/517 instead), bl_spi_protocol_get_command (:163, zero callers — bl_spi.c uses request->command directly), bl_spi_protocol_get_op_state (:225, zero callers). These are config-independent orphans (latent API surface), not config-gated. Dead STATE: seq_error_count is written (:121) but never read (see findings). Dead BRANCH: the 0xFF/0x00 test (:145) is behaviorally identical to the final else (:148).
test_coverage: INADEQUATE. Tests/unit/test_spi_protocol.c does not link this file — it tests parallel mock logic (format_response, parse_write_req_frame, get_cmd_info) that re-implements the protocol independently, so the real parser/builder/CRC are untested (confirmed: no test file references any bl_spi_protocol_* symbol). Concrete gaps for the real code: (1) bl_spi_protocol_crc8 has no known-answer vector; (2) bl_spi_protocol_process boundary cases — length < BL_SPI_FRAME_MIN_SIZE, data_len=255 max, expected_len underflow guard (line 94), poll-frame all-0xAA, legacy vs A+ detection, magic-but-truncated; (3) build_response/build_legacy_response padding-to-16 and CRC placement; (4) sequence-error path (line 117-124). This is the bootloader DFU framing that runs during a sealed-unit OTA — it should have direct coverage.

role: UART (LPUART1) DFU driver for the bootloader: init/deinit, IT-based RX ring buffer, AT+DFU line parser, and +DFU response formatter. Active only in the bootloader's UART-DFU path.
compiled_in: all (bootloader is built as a separate image, independent of APP/BOARD/COMM). The UART-DFU runtime path is reached for any board when the app requests DFU over UART or auto-detect resolves to UART. BL_UART_BAUDRATE is config-gated (9600 if BL_PROTOCOL_UART, else 115200, overridable via -DBL_UART_BAUDRATE).

findings.description: Four public functions are genuine orphans: no caller anywhere in the Bootloader tree (confirmed by grep over Bootloader/Src; they appear only as definitions, header decls and .map symbols). The UART-DFU consumer path uses bl_uart_process/bl_uart_get_command exclusively; raw byte/buffer reads, available-count, and deinit are never invoked. bl_uart_deinit being unused means the LPUART1 + PA2/PA3 AF config is never torn down before jump-to-app (see separate power finding).
findings.impact: No functional bug (dead, not mis-wired). Adds code size to a 32 KB bootloader region and presents an untested API surface (bl_uart_rx_available has a real off-by-context bug, below, that is masked only because it is dead).
findings.recommendation: Either remove the four unused functions, or document them as a deliberately-retained API. If kept, add unit tests so the latent bug in bl_uart_rx_available is not shipped as a trap for a future caller.

findings.description: Wrong byte-count for a wrapped ring when head==tail. The ring is empty iff head==tail, but this function returns head-tail only when head>tail. The head==tail (empty) case falls into the first branch and correctly returns 0. However the formula BL_RX_BUFFER_SIZE - tail + head for the wrapped case is correct only for a power-of-two-independent ring; with BL_RX_BUFFER_SIZE=1024 it is arithmetically fine. The real defect: the function reads volatile rx_head and rx_tail twice (once in the comparison, once in the arithmetic) without snapshotting. An ISR storing a byte between the two reads can change rx_head, yielding a count that is off by one or, in the wrapped branch, momentarily inconsistent.
findings.impact: Currently latent: the function is dead code (no caller). If revived, a caller could read a stale/over-large available count and over-read the ring. Low real-world impact today, medium if the API is reused.
findings.recommendation: Snapshot head/tail into locals once (with a short __disable_irq window or by reading head first then tail), compute from the snapshot. Add a unit test covering the wrapped case.

findings.description: Unconditional __disable_irq()/__enable_irq() pair. If this is ever called from a context where interrupts are already masked, the unconditional __enable_irq at the end re-enables them prematurely, breaking the caller's critical section. Today the only caller is bl_main.c:276 from the main thread with IRQs enabled, so it is safe — but the pattern is fragile.
findings.impact: No current bug. Becomes a real reentrancy hazard if flush is ever called from within a critical section or from an ISR.
findings.recommendation: Save/restore PRIMASK (uint32_t pm = __get_PRIMASK(); __disable_irq(); ...; __set_PRIMASK(pm);) instead of unconditional enable, to make the helper context-safe.

findings.description: Ring-overflow recovery does not resync the line parser. When rx_overflow is set (ISR dropped bytes because the 1024-byte ring filled while a flash write blocked the consumer), bl_uart_process clears the flag and the partial cmd_buffer (cmd_len=0) but then continues consuming the ring from wherever rx_tail points. Because bytes were silently dropped mid-line, the next bytes pulled are the middle of a WRITE payload, not a fresh 'AT+DFU=' line. Parsing resumes and only resynchronizes on the next CR/LF. The dropped bytes mean the *following* line is also corrupt (its head was eaten), so at least one good WRITE chunk is lost without the host being told — the host sees no +DFU response for that chunk and must time out / retry.
findings.impact: On a slow or jittery host that outruns the blocking flash write, a chunk can be dropped silently. The DFU transfer stalls until host retry/timeout rather than failing fast. In the sealed deployment the bootloader is only entered for a deliberate field-magnet-triggered update (rare), so blast radius is low, but a silent dropped chunk during a field reflash is exactly the kind of corruption that bricks a sealed unit if the host does not verify via VERIFY/CRC afterwards.
findings.recommendation: On rx_overflow, also discard the rest of the current partial line up to and including the next CR/LF before resuming (set a 'skip until newline' state), and emit a BUSY/overflow response so the host knows to back off and retry that chunk. The existing CRC VERIFY step is the backstop, but failing loud on overflow is safer than relying on it.

findings.location: bl_uart.c:125-132 (bl_uart_deinit unused) vs bl_main.c jump-to-app path
findings.description: bl_uart_deinit (which disables the LPUART1 IRQ, HAL_UART_DeInit, and returns PA2/PA3 to analog) is never called. On the UART-DFU success path the bootloader jumps to the application (BL_STATE_JUMP_APP) with LPUART1 still enabled, its IRQ still enabled in NVIC, and PA2/PA3 still in AF push-pull. The app re-inits its own UART so functionally this is overwritten, but the LPUART1_IRQn enable bit and any pending RXNE are carried across the jump before the app reconfigures NVIC/VTOR.
findings.impact: Minor. A spurious LPUART1 interrupt could fire against the app's (relocated) vector table in the narrow window between jump and the app's own UART/NVIC setup. Not a power-consumption issue at runtime (bootloader exits immediately on jump), but leaving the IRQ armed across a vector-table switch is a latent fault-handler risk.
findings.recommendation: Call bl_uart_stop_rx()/bl_uart_deinit() (or at least HAL_NVIC_DisableIRQ(LPUART1_IRQn)) on the BL_STATE_JUMP_APP transition before SCB->VTOR is switched, mirroring the SPI deinit already done on the SPI->jump path.

findings.description: The TX timeout comment (lines 188-190) hard-codes '9600 baud' reasoning but the formula correctly uses BL_UART_BAUDRATE, which can be 115200 (UW_DOPPLER/overridden builds). The comment is comment-rot: at 115200 the per-byte time is ~0.087ms not 1.04ms, so the prose no longer matches the code (the code is fine). Magic numbers 50/100/1000 ms are unexplained.
findings.impact: None functional; the formula is correct for any baud. Misleading comment for a future maintainer.
findings.recommendation: Reword the comment to not pin a specific baud, or compute the example from BL_UART_BAUDRATE. Name the 100/1000 ms clamp bounds as macros.

findings.description: The return value of the re-arming HAL_UART_Receive_IT at line 369 is discarded. If HAL returns HAL_BUSY/HAL_ERROR (e.g. an ORE/framing error left the handle in a non-READY state), reception silently stops: no further RxCplt callbacks, the ring goes quiet, and bl_uart_process spins forever returning false. There is no UART error callback (HAL_UART_ErrorCallback) defined, so ORE (overrun) — plausible at 115200 with a blocked consumer — is never cleared and RX dies.
findings.impact: In the sealed-deploy field-reflash scenario, a single overrun/framing glitch can permanently wedge UART RX for the rest of the bootloader session. The outer BL_DETECTION_TIMEOUT and CMD timeout in bl_main mitigate the detection phase, but once in BL_STATE_DFU_UART there is no watchdog visible here to recover a dead RX. Could hang the DFU session (host must power-cycle, which a sealed unit cannot do easily).
findings.recommendation: Check the re-arm return; on non-OK, clear error flags (__HAL_UART_CLEAR_OREFLAG etc.) and retry the Receive_IT, or implement HAL_UART_ErrorCallback to clear ORE/FE/NE and re-arm. Add a unit test that injects an overrun and asserts RX recovers.

findings.description: Bounds arithmetic in the printable-string branch (lines 313-320) is correct for the actual sizes (response_size=512, len after prefix=8, data_len<=512 from bl_dfu response buffer): worst case copy_len clamps to 501 and the trailing CRLF fits. The hex branch (323-326) guards with (len+3)<response_size per iteration, safe. The final transmit guard (351) correctly rejects negative snprintf returns. No overflow found. Noting the dependence on data_len never exceeding ~505 — this holds only because the response buffer is BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE and bl_dfu never returns more; there is no _Static_assert tying these together.
findings.impact: None currently. Fragile coupling: if a future DFU command returned a larger response_len than BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE, the printable clamp math (response_size - len - 3) is still safe (clamps down), but the unchecked assumption is worth pinning.
findings.recommendation: Add a comment or assert that data_len passed here is bounded by BL_TX_BUFFER_SIZE. No code change required.

findings.description: No unit tests exist for the bootloader UART parser. The line-assembly state machine has non-trivial edges that are exactly the brick-risk surface: (a) cmd_overflow drop-whole-line logic (233-247), (b) the trailing CR/LF strip loop (253-255), (c) the >=7 length + 'AT+DFU' prefix gate (258), (d) rx_overflow mid-line recovery (220-225), (e) send_response string-vs-hex classification and bounds. None of these are mocked/tested in Tests/unit (the bootloader is built as a separate image and the test harness targets the app).
findings.impact: The most fragile, corruption-prone logic in the bootloader (the thing that decides whether a WRITE line is acted on or dropped) has zero regression coverage. A refactor could silently re-introduce truncated-WRITE acceptance, which is a direct sealed-unit brick vector.
findings.recommendation: Add host-compilable unit tests for bl_uart_process (feed byte streams: complete line, split line, over-length line, embedded CR vs LF, overflow-then-recover) and bl_uart_send_response (OK/data string, OK/binary->hex, each error code, oversized data clamp). HAL_UART_* and the ring can be exercised by driving rx_buffer/rx_head directly since they are file-static — extract the parser or expose a test seam.

dead_code: Four genuine orphans (no caller in the entire Bootloader tree, verified by grep): bl_uart_read (162), bl_uart_read_byte (174), bl_uart_rx_available (153), bl_uart_deinit (125). These are not config-gated — they are dead in every build. The #if BL_UART_BAUDRATE==9600 banner blocks (116-120) are config-gated, not dead. All other functions are reachable: bl_uart_init/start_rx (bl_main.c:268-269), bl_uart_flush_rx (276), bl_uart_stop_rx (290,316), bl_uart_has_data (296), bl_uart_process (336), bl_uart_get_command (337), bl_uart_send_response (multiple), bl_uart_print (bl_main.c:574,580), bl_uart_transmit (via send_response/print), bl_uart_rx_irq_handler (via HAL_UART_RxCpltCallback), LPUART1_IRQHandler (vector). No unused statics/params spotted; rx_byte is written by HAL and read into the ring by the ISR handler (used).
test_coverage: Not covered. No Tests/unit coverage for the bootloader UART at all — the parser (bl_uart_process), command extraction (bl_uart_get_command), and response formatter (bl_uart_send_response) are pure, host-testable logic with brick-relevant edge cases (truncated/over-length line drop, CR/LF handling, AT+DFU prefix gate, overflow recovery, string-vs-hex response bounds) and none are exercised. This is the highest-value gap: see the test-gap finding. The HW glue (init/IRQ/transmit) is n/a for unit testing but the line state machine should be extracted/seamed and tested.

role: ADC1 driver: configures ADC on PA11/ADC_IN7 for the salt-water-switch (SWS) conductivity read, enables the VREFINT internal path for MGR_BAT's VDDA computation, and provides single-conversion polled reads (legacy 0-on-fail + status-returning variant). Channel is shared: MGR_BAT switches to VREFINT/IN0 and restores IN7.
compiled_in: Compiled in all configs (no #if guards in adc.c; symbols always linked). Functionally exercised only where BSP_HAS_VBAT_ADC / SWS exist; MX_ADC_Init/DeInit are called under USE_UW_DOPPLER_APP (main.c:836, lpm.c STOP path, mgr_lpm_uw.c STOP2/SHUTDOWN). Sealed target APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART exercises this file fully.

findings.description: ADC_ReadValue() (legacy 0-on-failure wrapper) has no live caller anywhere in the firmware. Grep over the whole tree finds it only in its own definition/declaration and the stale audit doc. The only live reader is mgr_sws.c:492 which calls ADC_ReadValueChecked().
findings.impact: None functional. It is a genuine orphan (public API kept 'for compatibility' but unused), not config-gated. Minor: it keeps the misleading 'returns 0 on error' contract alive and costs a few bytes of flash.
findings.recommendation: Either remove ADC_ReadValue()+its prototype, or add a comment that it is retained as a deliberately-unused legacy API. If kept, do not let new code adopt it (it reintroduces the failure==0 ambiguity the checked variant exists to fix).

findings.description: The block comment states ADC_ReadValueChecked returns false 'on a HAL failure (start/poll error or an error-latched handle)'. The function never inspects hadc.State / hadc.ErrorCode. HAL_ADC_Start() (Drivers stm32wlxx_hal_adc.c:1147) does not gate on a pre-existing HAL_ADC_STATE_ERROR_* bit and in fact calls ADC_CLEAR_ERRORCODE on a successful enable. So a previously error-latched-but-now-enableable handle returns true, not false.
findings.impact: Comment overstates the guarantee. No corruption: a truly broken ADC still fails ADC_Enable/poll and returns false, so the SWS hold-last-sample safety still works. Risk is a future reader trusting the comment and skipping an explicit state check they actually needed.
findings.recommendation: Reword the comment to 'returns false if HAL_ADC_Start or HAL_ADC_PollForConversion report an error', or add an explicit `if (HAL_ADC_GetState(&hadc) & HAL_ADC_STATE_ERROR_INTERNAL) return false;` if a latched-error rejection is genuinely wanted.

findings.description: Calibration failure path calls Error_Handler() then `return`. The init also returns silently after HAL_ADC_Init failure (line 38-41). Error_Handler() in this firmware (main.c) is the de-facto reset/hang path, so the trailing `return` is normally unreachable — but if Error_Handler is ever made non-fatal, MX_ADC_Init would return with hadc in a partially-configured/uncalibrated state and the next ADC read would still 'succeed' with a bad calibration factor.
findings.impact: In the sealed deployment a hard ADC fault correctly funnels to Error_Handler (reset). Latent: the silent `return` after Error_Handler is defensive dead code that hides a half-init handle if Error_Handler semantics change. Calibration is single-ended-only on WL (signature takes no SingleEnded arg) so that part is correct.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as-is given Error_Handler() never returns. If you want belt-and-suspenders, drop the unreachable `return;` lines (they are dead) or convert MX_ADC_Init to return a status so callers can react instead of relying on Error_Handler being terminal.

findings.description: Channel mapping verified against DS13105 (datasheet): PA11 = ADC_IN7 (line 3382) so SWS using ADC_CHANNEL_7 is CORRECT; PB13 = ADC_IN0 (line 3359) so MGR_BAT using ADC_CHANNEL_0 is CORRECT. This directly CONTRADICTS docs/reports/adc_audit.md:34 which claims 'PB13 = ADC_IN5' — that prior finding is factually wrong (PB1=ADC_IN5, line 3324). VREFEN via ADC_COMMON->CCR (line 48) matches CMSIS (stm32wl55xx.h:1101/1881).
findings.impact: No bug here — this is a positive confirmation. The risk is the stale, wrong adc_audit.md/MASTER_AUDIT references misleading a future change to 'fix' the channel to IN5, which would break VBAT.
findings.recommendation: Correct or annotate docs/reports/adc_audit.md (line 34) and MASTER_AUDIT to mark the PB13=ADC_IN5 claim as retracted. Optionally add a `_Static_assert`-style comment or a #define mapping (ADC_CHANNEL_SWS / ADC_CHANNEL_VBAT) so the verified mapping is self-documenting in code.

findings.description: MX_ADC_DeInit ignores the HAL_ADC_DeInit() return value. If DeInit fails (e.g. a conversion is mid-flight and ADC_ConversionStop times out), VREFEN was already cleared (line 73) but the peripheral may be left partially enabled going into STOP2/SHUTDOWN. MspDeInit (line 96) does __HAL_RCC_ADC_CLK_DISABLE + HAL_GPIO_DeInit(PA11) which is the right teardown, but only runs if HAL_ADC_DeInit reaches the Msp callback.
findings.impact: In the sealed STOP2 loop a stuck DeInit would leave the ADC drawing its bias (~µA) for that sleep window; it would self-correct on the next wake's MX_ADC_Init. Low probability (single-conversion, software-trigger, no DMA, conversion is stopped by ADC_ReadValueChecked before sleep), low energy impact. No brick.
findings.recommendation: Either check HAL_ADC_DeInit's return and on !HAL_OK force `__HAL_RCC_ADC_CLK_DISABLE()` directly, or document that the GPIO_DisableAllToAnalogInput + clock-gate downstream covers a failed DeInit. Not urgent.

findings.description: SamplingTimeCommon1 and SamplingTimeCommon2 are both set to 160.5 cycles, and every channel (SWS IN7, VBAT IN0, VREFINT) uses ADC_SAMPLINGTIME_COMMON_1. VREFINT on STM32WL needs >=4us sampling; 160.5 cycles at the configured PCLK/4 clock is adequate, but the two common slots being identical means there is no provision for a longer sample on the high-impedance VBAT divider (Thevenin ~86k) vs the SWS node.
