findings.description: MGR_PMLOG_get assumes the first s_valid_count slots are contiguous valid entries from slot 0 ('no holes possible in append-only flash'). The SF-1 torn-write fix in this same file DELIBERATELY creates holes: a torn write leaves a slot with EMPTY magic but programmed dw1 (a 'wasted' slot) and the next log skips past it to a later slot, so a VALID entry can sit at a higher index than an EMPTY/wasted slot. get(index) returns slot_at(index) directly. Example: slots 0,1 VALID, slot 2 torn (magic=EMPTY, garbage payload), slot 3 VALID -> init sets s_valid_count=3, but get(2) returns slot_at(2) = the torn slot (EMPTY magic + uninitialised-looking payload) and slot 3's real data is never returned. The contiguity comment directly contradicts the torn-slot handling elsewhere in the file.
findings.impact: On the sealed deployment, AT+PMLOG=? is the ONLY way to read forensic data off a recovered tag. After any brownout-torn flash write (precisely the failure mode this log exists to capture), the dump prints a garbage/zeroed row for the torn slot and silently drops the most recent real ERROR entry. The post-mortem becomes unreliable exactly in the scenario it was built for. Not a brick, but defeats the feature's purpose.
findings.recommendation: Make get() iterate slots skipping non-VALID-magic ones and return the index-th VALID slot (filter on e->magic==MGR_PMLOG_MAGIC_VALID), OR have init record the ordered list of valid slot indices. Update/remove the 'no holes possible' comment which is now false. Add a unit test with a torn slot between two valid slots asserting get(k) maps to the k-th valid entry.

findings.description: When the page is fully populated (no truly-empty slot found), init sets s_next_slot=0 but does NOT reset s_valid_count or s_next_seq, and leaves the cursor at 0 'to trigger an erase on next write'. The next MGR_PMLOG_log then walks the skip loop (152-154): slot 0 is not truly-empty, so it advances all the way to MAX_ENTRIES and erases (correct). BUT until that next log fires, MGR_PMLOG_count() reports s_valid_count (e.g. 128) while s_next_slot=0 — internally inconsistent state. More importantly, if MGR_PMLOG_log's erase succeeds it calls pmlog_erase_page() which resets counts, but the skip-loop pre-increment means after erase s_next_slot=0 and the entry is written at slot 0 (correct). The window is small but the cursor=0/count=128 intermediate state is fragile and only works because no reader runs between init and the next log.
findings.impact: Low real-world impact on the single-threaded baremetal flow, but the invariant 's_next_slot points at where the next write goes' is violated (it points at a full slot). Any future reader/refactor that trusts s_next_slot as a free-slot pointer (rather than relying on the skip loop) would write over slot 0 without erasing.
findings.recommendation: Either keep cursor at MGR_PMLOG_MAX_ENTRIES (the genuine-wrap sentinel the log loop already handles at 157) instead of forcing it to 0, or add a comment that 0 here is a 'force-wrap' sentinel, not a free slot. Prefer leaving it at MAX_ENTRIES so the log path's wrap branch is the single erase trigger.

findings.location: mgr_pmlog.c:182 and 164-165 (seq), header field uint16_t seq at mgr_pmlog.h:51
findings.description: seq is 16-bit but the page only holds 128 entries and is erased on every wrap, so seq is reset to 0 each erase (pmlog_erase_page line 69 and init line 80). s_next_seq is capped at 0xFFFF (line 182 'if (s_next_seq < 0xFFFFu) s_next_seq++'). Because the page erases at 128 entries, s_next_seq in practice never approaches 0xFFFF, so the cap is effectively dead defensive code — fine. However init's max_seq logic (line 88 'if (e->seq >= max_seq) max_seq = e->seq') combined with s_next_seq = max_seq+1 (line 109) silently overflows if max_seq==0xFFFF (max_seq+1 wraps to 0). Unreachable given the erase-per-128 design, but the seq is documented as 'monotonic within the page' and the only thing that guarantees monotonicity is the erase, not the type. The 0xFFFF cap and the seq width are mismatched intent vs a 128-entry page.
findings.impact: No live defect (erase bounds seq well under 0xFFFF). Pure latent/dead-defensive inconsistency; would only matter if MAX_ENTRIES grew past 65535 without an erase, which the design forbids.
findings.recommendation: Either drop the 0xFFFF cap (seq is page-local and erase-bounded) or document that the cap is belt-and-suspenders for a never-erased page. Optionally narrow seq to uint8_t plus a wrap flag if space is needed; not required.

findings.location: mgr_pmlog.c:144-189 (MGR_PMLOG_log) reached from mgr_evtlog.c:80; and mgr_lpm_uw.c:900
findings.description: MGR_PMLOG_log unlocks flash and issues two blocking HAL_FLASH_Program double-word writes (~tens of us each, plus possible page erase ~25ms) with no critical section. It is invoked from MGR_EVTLOG_log, which is plausibly callable from error/fault paths. If MGR_EVTLOG_log (hence PMLOG) can ever be entered from an ISR or from an error handler that itself can be re-entered while a flash op is mid-flight, the FLASH controller is left half-configured (unlocked, CR programmed) and concurrent flash access (incl. code execution if code ran from this bank, which it does not here since app runs from main bank but PMLOG page is in the same flash interface) would stall the bus. No locking/re-entrancy guard exists.
findings.impact: On baremetal single main loop this is currently safe. Risk is config/refactor-dependent: if an error event is logged from an ISR (e.g. a fault or RTC ISR mirroring an ERROR), a flash program could be interrupted and another HAL_FLASH_Program re-entered, corrupting the FLASH->CR sequence. The whole flash interface stalls reads during program/erase on STM32WL — a 25ms erase blocks any other flash read including interrupt vectors fetched from flash.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether MGR_EVTLOG_log (ERROR severity) can fire from ISR/fault context in the UW_DOPPLER build. If yes, guard MGR_PMLOG_log with a re-entrancy flag (skip if already inside a flash op) or defer flash writes to main-loop context. At minimum document the 'main-context only' precondition in the header.

findings.description: MGR_LOG_ERR/WARN/INFO are called immediately after HAL_FLASH_Lock() returns in error paths (e.g. pmlog_erase_page 63, program_two_dwords 137). These are post-lock, so flash is locked — OK. But MGR_LOG_* in this module may route to UART/console which on the sealed DEBUG=0 build is torn down (per prod_uart_teardown memory: DEBUG=0 kills the console). The log calls then do nothing useful and just cost cycles/stack in the flash failure path. Not a defect, but the operator-facing diagnostics here are invisible in the production sealed build — the only failure record would be... the PMLOG itself, which just failed to write.
findings.impact: In the sealed DEBUG=0 deployment, a flash erase/program failure in PMLOG produces no observable signal (console dead, and the failure is the log subsystem itself). Silent loss of forensic capability with no fallback indicator. Low because flash failures are rare and non-fatal to operation.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as-is, but consider setting a sticky RAM/retention flag or an EVTLOG (SRAM) entry on PMLOG flash failure so at least the volatile log records that the persistent log failed. Document that PMLOG self-failure is otherwise unobservable in production.

findings.description: Validity rests entirely on a 32-bit magic 0x504D4C45. There is no CRC/checksum over the 16-byte entry. A bit-flip in the payload (tick/seq/data) of an otherwise-valid slot is undetectable; a random 32-bit pattern in a corrupt page that happens to equal the magic is treated as VALID and dumped. init only flags 'neither VALID nor EMPTY' magic as corruption (line 96-99); a slot whose magic accidentally equals VALID but whose data is garbage passes. For a forensic log this is a minor integrity gap.
findings.impact: Low: corrupted-but-magic-matching entries dump as plausible-looking garbage during AT+PMLOG. No operational risk; only mild forensic ambiguity. Probability of a 32-bit collision is ~2^-32 per slot.
findings.recommendation: Optional: add a 1-byte XOR/CRC of the entry into the reserved field (currently always 0, line 169) and validate it in init/get. Low priority given the reserved byte is free and currently wasted.

findings.description: Comment-rot: the MGR_PMLOG_get comment asserts 'The first index valid_count entries are guaranteed contiguous from slot 0 (no holes possible in append-only flash)'. This was true before the SF-1 torn-write fix but is now false (torn/wasted slots create holes). The comment actively misleads a future reader into trusting linear indexing. (Root cause of the high-severity finding above; called out separately as a doc defect.)
findings.impact: Misleading documentation that masks the get() hole bug; a maintainer reading only the comment would not realise indexing is broken after a tear.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the comment to state that holes ARE possible (torn slots) and that get() must filter by VALID magic, once the get() fix lands.

findings.description: test_pmlog_torn.c covers the torn-write/skip/wrap state machine well (4 checks) but does NOT exercise MGR_PMLOG_get / oldest-first read-back AT ALL, and specifically not the case of a torn (hole) slot preceding a valid slot during read. The exact high-severity bug (get() returning the torn slot instead of the next valid entry) is untested. There is also no test for MGR_PMLOG_init's s_valid_count vs reachable-via-get count consistency after a tear. The test mirrors a private reimplementation rather than calling the real functions, so a real-function regression in get()/init() would not be caught.
findings.impact: The reliability-critical read path (the only way to extract field forensics) has zero coverage; the contiguity bug shipped untested.
findings.recommendation: Add a test (ideally exercising the real MGR_PMLOG_get over a mocked flash array) for: (1) get over a page with a torn slot between valids returns the k-th VALID entry, (2) count()==number of entries get() can return without NULL/garbage, (3) init after reboot with a torn-among-valid layout yields a consistent count/get mapping.

dead_code: No genuine orphans inside the file — every static (slot_at, slot_dw1, slot_is_truly_empty, pmlog_erase_page, program_two_dwords) and every public function has a live caller. Config-gated reachability: the whole module's write path is only reachable under USE_UW_DOPPLER_APP (mgr_evtlog.c:78-83 #if gate; mgr_lpm_uw.c is UW-only); init/get/count/clear are reachable only via the UW_DOPPLER AT-command table. So in non-UW builds the code links and runs init() (called from kns_app_uw_doppler.c which itself is UW-only) — effectively the entire file is live ONLY in the UW_DOPPLER config and dormant (linked, never invoked) elsewhere. Near-dead defensive branch: the s_next_seq 0xFFFF cap (line 182) and init max_seq+1 (line 109) are unreachable in practice because the page erases every 128 entries, keeping seq far below 0xFFFF (config-independent design invariant, intentional belt-and-suspenders). entry.reserved is written 0 and never read (intentional 16-byte padding, not dead).
test_coverage: Partial. Tests/unit/test_pmlog_torn.c covers the torn-write skip/no-erase/genuine-wrap/init-skip state machine via a faithful private reimplementation (good for the write cursor logic). GAPS: (1) MGR_PMLOG_get oldest-first read-back is entirely untested, including the high-severity hole case where a torn slot precedes a valid one and get() returns the torn slot / drops the last valid entry; (2) no test that count() equals the number of non-NULL, non-garbage entries get() yields after a tear; (3) tests reimplement the logic rather than calling the real functions, so a regression in the actual mgr_pmlog.c get()/init() would not be caught. The read path — the sole forensic extraction mechanism for the sealed deployment — needs direct coverage.

role: Persistent sliding-window TX rate limiter: caps TX bursts over a configurable rolling window as a last-resort battery-drain defence; ring of monotonic-second timestamps in SRAM2 retention RAM, CRC32-validated, with a wrap-safe HAL_GetTick-derived clock.
compiled_in: Built whenever mgr_rate.c is in the source set. Functionally exercised only in APP=UW_DOPPLER (sole caller is kns_app_uw_doppler.c + the UW_DOPPLER AT-cmd list + NVM gather/apply). Not referenced by STDLN/GUI/DOPPLER app code, so in those configs the object compiles but is dead (orphan at link unless GC'd).

findings.description: The only unit test that exercises the rate limiter RE-IMPLEMENTS the logic as a local copy (RATE_CAP=100, hand-copied rate_nowS/rate_trim/rate_record/rate_blocked) instead of compiling and linking the real mgr_rate.c. It never calls MGR_RATE_init/recordTx/isBlocked/setConfig/clear. Consequence: ring_valid(), rate_crc32()/ring_crc(), the reinit-on-corruption path in MGR_RATE_init (lines 100-112), ring_oldest() modular indexing (119-122), isBlocked()'s retry_in_s computation (166-171), setConfig() clamping (177-186), and MGR_RATE_clear() have ZERO coverage against the shipped code.
findings.impact: A regression in the real code (e.g. a wrong offsetof in ring_crc, an off-by-one in ring_oldest, a sign error in retry_in_s) would pass CI because the test validates a divergent copy. For a sealed 12-month deployment this is the firmware's last-line anti-drain defence — silent breakage is high-consequence.
findings.recommendation: Add a unit test that #includes/links the real mgr_rate.c with mocked HAL_GetTick + MGR_LOG, then asserts: cold-init clears a corrupt ring; CRC corruption forces reinit; recordTx/isBlocked enforce the limit at exactly max_tx; retry_in_s equals window-elapsed; setConfig clamps each of the 4 bounds; clear() zeroes count but keeps config; ring_oldest correctness at count==MAX_CAP.

findings.description: MGR_RATE_nowS mutates module statics mono_s/mono_last_ms/mono_rem_ms with no atomicity and is not reentrant. All current callers are in main/MAC-event context (verified: kns_app_uw_doppler.c:1471 KNS_MAC_TX_DONE handler, :2442 MONITORING loop, :1663 init; AT-cmd handlers; NVM gather), so no race exists today.
findings.impact: No current bug. But if any future code calls MGR_RATE_nowS / recordTx / isBlocked from an ISR or a second context, the read-modify-write of the clock and ring would race and could corrupt the monotonic clock or ring.count (which then defeats the rate cap or freezes the quota).
findings.recommendation: Document the 'main-context only, non-reentrant' contract in mgr_rate.h, or guard the clock update + ring mutation with a brief __disable_irq/__enable_irq critical section if ISR use is ever anticipated.

findings.description: The wrap-safe clock requires at least one MGR_RATE_nowS call per 49.7-day HAL_GetTick wrap; a longer gap under-counts elapsed time. In the sealed UW_DOPPLER duty cycle the device spends long stretches in STOP2/SHUTDOWN where HAL_GetTick is frozen/reset and no nowS call occurs.
findings.impact: Conservative-only: a missed wrap makes ring entries look younger, so the window never releases EARLY (it can only hold TX back longer, never let extra TX through). Safe direction for a drain limiter, but means the effective window can stretch unpredictably after very long sleeps. Not a brick/corruption risk.
findings.recommendation: No code change required; the conservative direction is acceptable. Note this clock-vs-sleep coupling in the header so a future maintainer doesn't 'fix' it into an unsafe direction.

findings.description: The .c comment says state 'lives in SRAM2 retention so it survives resets'. .retentionRamBss is zeroed by Sram2_Init on BOR/NRST(PIN)/OBL (it survives only IWDG/SFT), as the header correctly documents (mgr_rate.h:13-15) and as the design relies on (magic/CRC catch the wipe → reinit). The .c wording is looser than the header.
findings.impact: Documentation only; behaviour is correct (cold-wipe -> magic mismatch -> clean reinit). Risk is a future reader over-trusting persistence.
findings.recommendation: Align the .c comment with the header: '.retentionRamBss survives IWDG/SFT only; BOR/NRST/OBL re-run Sram2_Init which zeroes it — magic+CRC then trigger reinit.'

findings.description: Uses GNU __typeof__ and relies on crc32 being the LAST struct member so offsetof(...,crc32) equals 'everything but the CRC'. This is correct today but is an implicit structural invariant with no compile-time guard. Also MGR_RATE_MAX_CAP (256) doubles as MGR_RATE_MAX_MAX_TX; the ring caps count at MAX_CAP so max_tx==256 is exactly reachable — fine, but coincidental coupling.
findings.impact: If a field is ever appended after crc32, ring_crc would silently CRC the wrong span and every boot would reinit (quota reset each boot = anti-drain defence weakened). Low probability, high-ish consequence for a sealed unit.
findings.recommendation: Add a _Static_assert that crc32 is the final member (e.g. assert offsetof(crc32)+sizeof(crc32)==sizeof(ring)), and keep the toolchain GNU-only assumption explicit (the codebase already uses GCC, so __typeof__/offsetof are fine).

dead_code: No genuine orphan within the file: every static (rate_crc32, ring_crc, ring_commit, ring_valid, ring_oldest, trim_window) and every public API is reachable from the UW_DOPPLER call graph (kns_app_uw_doppler.c, mgr_at_cmd_list_uw_doppler.c, mgr_nvm.c). At the CONFIG level the whole translation unit is config-gated: in APP=STDLN/GUI/DOPPLER there are no callers, so the object is effectively dead there (intentional — UW_DOPPLER-only feature, not an orphan). No unreachable branches; no unused params/returns (all void/used).
test_coverage: Partially covered, but NOT against the real code. Tests/unit/test_wrap_overflow.c reproduces the monotonic-clock + trim logic as a hand-copied mirror (different CAP, reimplemented functions) and validates tick-wrap and warm-reset behaviour of THAT copy. The shipped mgr_rate.c is never compiled into a test. Concrete gaps with zero coverage on real code: CRC32/ring_valid corruption detection and reinit, MGR_RATE_init cold-vs-warm resume, isBlocked retry_in_s math, setConfig 4-way clamping, MGR_RATE_clear, ring_oldest at count==MAX_CAP, and the NVM 0/0-sentinel apply path interaction (mgr_nvm.c:480).

role: Reed-switch (magnet) driver + power-latch GPIO for SMD_STDALONE: poll-based asymmetric debouncer, single-context event ring, EXTI wake-only ISR, TX-transient blanking window.
compiled_in: BOARD=SMD_STDALONE (BSP_HAS_REED_SWITCH=1) → full driver; all other boards (SMD_PA/SMD_NOPA/SMD_OP, BSP_HAS_REED_SWITCH undefined) → the no-op stub block (lines 346-355). Sealed target APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE compiles the full driver.

findings.description: HAL_GPIO_EXTI_Callback increments g_reed_isr_count for ANY GPIO_Pin BEFORE the `if (GPIO_Pin != REED_MCU_Pin) return;` filter at line 334. The counter is documented (lines 300-303) and named as a reed-fire diagnostic, but it actually counts every EXTI callback invocation. Currently harmless because the file comment (lines 20-22) and MGR_REED_init only ever configure the reed pin for EXTI in this build, so no other line reaches this callback.
findings.impact: Latent: if any future peripheral is given an EXTI line sharing EXTI9_5 (PB6 default) or another line routed through HAL_GPIO_EXTI_IRQHandler, g_reed_isr_count would silently over-count and the heartbeat reed-activity diagnostic in kns_app_uw_doppler.c would read wrong. No functional/brick impact in the current sealed config.
findings.recommendation: Move `g_reed_isr_count++;` after the pin filter (below line 335) so it only counts genuine reed edges, matching its documented contract.

findings.description: No unit test exercises the actual driver logic. Tests/unit/test_reed_hold_actions.c only re-implements a COPY of the hold-duration classify logic that lives in the app (kns_app_uw_doppler.c), not mgr_reed.c. The load-bearing logic here — asymmetric debounce (5 vs 20 samples), candidate-reset-on-bounce (lines 203-211), the 10 ms rate-limit, the TX-blank freeze (lines 180-187), isDebouncing() semantics, ring-full drop, and last_hold_ms computation with rising_tick==0 guard (line 231) — is entirely untested.
findings.impact: Regressions in the debouncer or blanking (both safety-relevant: they gate gesture detection AND the LPM STOP2 re-entry decision via isDebouncing) would not be caught by CI. A broken debounce could either swallow a real magnet (sealed unit unrecoverable) or chatter the gesture FSM to a spurious power-off.
findings.recommendation: Add Tests/unit/test_reed_debounce.c that compiles mgr_reed.c against mocked HAL_GetTick/HAL_GPIO_ReadPin: assert ON confirms at exactly 5 samples, OFF at 20, a 1-sample glitch resets the counter, blankUntil() freezes sampling and forces isDebouncing()==false, ring drops the 9th event without overwrite, and last_hold_ms is 0 when no prior rising edge.

findings.description: MGR_REED_isDebouncing() reads s_candidate_state/s_confirmed_state but, unlike isMagnetPresent() and getEvent(), does NOT call reed_poll() first. Its returned value is therefore only as fresh as the last poll driven by another accessor. The blank-window correctness (blanking must force isDebouncing()==false, per header lines 39-44 and the LPM gate) depends on reed_poll() having run during the blank to collapse candidate→confirmed (lines 182-183). In the current main loop MGR_GESTURE_task() (kns_app_uw_doppler.c:1887) drives a poll early, before idleTick (line 2494) calls isDebouncing(), so it works — but the invariant is implicit and undocumented.
findings.impact: Fragile coupling: if the call ordering changes (e.g. idleTick reached on a loop path where no getEvent/isMagnetPresent ran that iteration), isDebouncing() could return a stale `true` during a blank window and needlessly hold the chip awake (power), or stale `false` and allow STOP2 re-entry mid-debounce (missed magnet edge — the exact failure the function exists to prevent).
findings.recommendation: Make isDebouncing() self-poll (call reed_poll() at entry) for symmetry with the other accessors, or document the 'must poll before querying' precondition in the header and at the LPM call site.

findings.description: s_blank_until_tick and s_blank_active are declared volatile (implying ISR sharing) but are only ever written by MGR_REED_blankUntil() and read/written by reed_poll(), both strictly main-context (blankUntil called from kns_app_uw_doppler.c:1885, reed_poll only from the main-context accessors). The two stores in blankUntil are also non-atomic w.r.t. each other, which would be a (benign here) torn-update concern only if an ISR did read them.
findings.impact: None functional. The misleading volatile signals a cross-context contract that does not exist, and forces the compiler to reload on every access in the hot poll path (negligible cost). Comment at lines 23-24 already acknowledges the ring's volatile is 'belt-and-suspenders, not load-bearing'.
findings.recommendation: Drop volatile on the two blank-window variables (they are single-context), or add a one-line note that volatile is defensive only, consistent with the ring-buffer comment.

findings.description: last_hold_ms = (now - rising_tick) uses HAL_GetTick() (ms) subtraction. rising_tick is set at the confirmed ON edge and zeroed at OFF; the (r != 0u) guard correctly yields 0 when no prior ON was seen. Unsigned wraparound of the 32-bit tick is handled correctly by the subtraction, but a hold spanning the full 49.7-day tick rollover would still be measured correctly only for a single wrap — not a concern for a gesture hold (max seconds).
findings.impact: None in practice: gesture holds are seconds-scale; the value feeds hold-duration classification (capped at >=10 s shutdown). No defect.
findings.recommendation: No action; noted for completeness.

dead_code: No genuine orphans. The no-reed stub block (lines 346-355) is config-gated dead on SMD_STDALONE (BSP_HAS_REED_SWITCH=1) but live on the other boards — intentional. The BSP_REED_ON_WKUP3 branch (lines 103-104, 314-318) and the BSP_REED_WKUP3_PARALLEL block (lines 133-142) are bench-mod-gated (not defined in the sealed build) — intentional config alternatives, not orphans. All public API functions have live callers (mgr_gesture.c, mgr_lpm_uw.c, kns_app_uw_doppler.c, mgr_at_cmd_list_uw_doppler.c). g_reed_isr_count/g_reed_isr_last_state are read by the heartbeat in kns_app_uw_doppler.c:1826-1827. reed_poll() is static and used. No unused statics, params, or ignored returns.
test_coverage: Inadequate for the testable logic. The debouncer state machine, event ring, blanking window, and last_hold_ms are pure functions of (mocked) HAL_GetTick + HAL_GPIO_ReadPin and SHOULD be unit-tested but are NOT — Tests/unit/test_reed_hold_actions.c only tests a duplicated copy of app-side hold classification, never linking or exercising mgr_reed.c. Concrete gaps: 5-vs-20 asymmetric confirmation thresholds, bounce-reset on candidate flip (lines 203-211), 10 ms rate-limit, blankUntil() freeze + isDebouncing()==false during blank, ring-full drop without overwrite, rising_tick==0 guard. The GPIO/EXTI/NVIC init and ISR are HW glue (n/a for unit test).

role: SPI command manager: drives the pipelined single-transaction SPI host protocol (poll DMA, parse A+/legacy frame, dispatch to handler table, build response) and maps Kineis MAC service events to MACStatus codes the SPI master polls.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only (Makefile:412-427 gate the whole MGR_SPI_CMD dir on -DUSE_SPI_DRIVER; kns_app.c:365-399 gate the calls on USE_SPI_DRIVER). NOT compiled in the sealed deployment target (APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART) — that build uses MGR_AT_CMD instead. App-agnostic within COMM=SPI (STDLN/GUI/UW_DOPPLER/DOPPLER).

findings.description: MGR_SPI_CMD_macEvtProcess dereferences spUserDataMsg (->bIsToBeTransmit, ->u8Attr.sf) and asserts it non-NULL for TX/RX terminal events. spUserDataMsg comes from USERDATA_txFifoGetFirst() which returns sUserDataTxFifo.spFirst (user_data.c:338-341), NULL when the FIFO is empty. If the MAC posts a TX_DONE/TXACK_DONE/TX_TIMEOUT/RX_ERROR/RX_TIMEOUT event while the TX FIFO is empty (stale/duplicate event after the element was already removed, or an unsolicited RX event mis-routed into the TX-completion group), kns_assert(spUserDataMsg != NULL) at line 324 fires. kns_assert_failed() (kns_assert.c:50-65) calls Error_Handler() => full firmware reset.
findings.impact: On a COMM=SPI unit, a single unexpected/duplicate MAC terminal event with an empty FIFO reboots the firmware. Not in the sealed UART image, but a self-induced reset/brick-loop risk for any SPI-host deployment; the assert is a hard reset, not a recoverable error.
findings.recommendation: Replace the asserts with a graceful guard: if spUserDataMsg == NULL, log, set macStatus to a defined code and return KNS_STATUS_OK without dereferencing or removing a FIFO element. An assert in a lifelong async event handler must not be able to reset the chip on a benign event ordering.

findings.description: macStatusAcknowledged is documented as the latch that keeps a terminal MAC status (TX_DONE etc.) until the master acknowledges it, to survive SPI desync. It is written here and in mgr_spi_cmd_list_general.c:367 / mgr_spi_cmd_list_user_data.c:272,278,287, but NEVER read as a condition anywhere in the tree (verified: no read/compare exists). The MACSTATUS handler (mgr_spi_cmd_list_general.c:88-105) returns macStatus unconditionally and its reset-after-read is commented out, so the latch the comment promises does not exist.
findings.impact: Dead state plus rotted comment: the documented anti-desync guarantee is not implemented. A reader trusts a protection that is not there. No runtime effect today, but it masks a real gap (terminal status can be overwritten by the next event before the master polls it).
findings.recommendation: Either implement the latch (MACSTATUS read clears terminal status only when acknowledged; refuse to overwrite an unacknowledged terminal status) or delete the variable and the misleading comment.

findings.description: Response arming happens up to three times per command. Handlers call bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread() (e.g. mgr_spi_cmd_list_general.c:61) which builds the A+ frame in txBuf (common.c:114-167) but via the legacy macro bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_read also maps to MCU_SPI_DRIVER_read (mcu_spi_driver.h:167) which actually re-arms the DMA. Then MGR_SPI_CMD_process_cmd (line 94-96) calls MCU_SPI_DRIVER_set_response(txBuf.data, txBuf.next_req). Then state_handler (line 253) calls MCU_SPI_DRIVER_read() again. The pipelined model and the legacy writeread model are mixed; the ordering between set_response (copies into spiTxBuf) and read() (arms DMA on spiTxBuf) is fragile.
findings.impact: Latent response-corruption / off-by-one-transaction race on COMM=SPI: the master can receive a stale idle frame or a half-updated TX buffer if the re-arm and set_response interleave with a fast master clock. Works on the bench at 125 kHz with NOP polling but is not robust.
findings.recommendation: Pick one model. In the pipelined design the handler should only fill txBuf.data/next_req and never call read(); the single re-arm belongs in state_handler after set_response. Ensure the legacy writeread->read macro does not arm DMA from inside a handler.

findings.description: spiState/cmdInProgress/macStatus are volatile but only touched in the main loop (kns_app.c:397-398); the ISR (HAL_SPI_TxRxCpltCallback/ErrorCallback) writes only startTickTimeout and spi_stats. Real cross-context sharing is spi_stats fields: ++ from both ISR (mcu_spi_driver.c:94-95,121) and main (mgr_spi_cmd.c:266) with no critical section (non-atomic RMW). The SPI_ENTER/EXIT_CRITICAL macros (mcu_spi_driver.h:53-54) exist but are unused.
findings.impact: spi_stats counters can lose an increment under an ISR/main race. Diagnostics-only, no functional impact.
findings.recommendation: Accept and document the stat imprecision, or guard the main-loop ++ with the existing critical-section macros. No correctness change needed.

findings.description: MGR_SPI_CMD_process_transaction unconditionally reads data[0..4] in the MGR_LOG_DEBUG at 118-119. The only caller guards with bytes_received >= SPI_FRAME_MIN_SIZE (5), so it is in-bounds today, and bytes_received is capped by DMA size SPI_TRANSACTION_SIZE=64 within rxBuf (256B), so no overflow. But the function is not self-defending against a future short-len caller.
findings.impact: No current overflow (caller-guarded); minor latent over-read if reused with a short buffer. The print is compiled out when DEBUG=0.
findings.recommendation: Add a len>=SPI_FRAME_MIN_SIZE guard inside the function before the 5-byte debug print so it is robust independent of the caller.

findings.description: DEBUG-gated direct-UART trace for cmd 0x3F (DFU_ENTER) uses magic literal 0x3F instead of CMD_DFU_ENTER (mgr_spi_cmd_list.h:98) and declares `extern UART_HandleTypeDef hlpuart1;` locally rather than via a header. It is #ifdef DEBUG so it does not ship in DEBUG=0 prod builds, but per CLAUDE.md debug markers should be removed with the root-cause fix.
findings.impact: Cosmetic/maintainability; no runtime effect in prod. Magic number rots if CMD_DFU_ENTER changes value.
findings.recommendation: Use CMD_DFU_ENTER, move the hlpuart1 extern to a shared header, and consider removing the trace once DFU entry is validated.

findings.location: mgr_spi_cmd.c:115-170, 278-503 (Tests/unit has only test_spi_protocol.c, covering mgr_spi_protocol.c)
findings.description: The complex testable logic here, the MGR_SPI_CMD_macEvtProcess event->MACStatus mapping switch (TX/RX/DL/SAT events, v11.1.0 KNS_MAC_TX_ABORT->MAC_RF_ABORTED mapping, NULL-guard behavior, FIFO-removal correctness) and the process_transaction/process_cmd dispatch (cmd bounds 0<cmd<SPICMD_MAX_COUNT, NULL handler, A+ vs legacy routing), has no unit test. test_spi_protocol.c references none of these functions (verified).
findings.impact: Regressions in event mapping (a future MAC ABI shift re-routing an event, or the empty-FIFO assert) ship undetected. Given the recent v11.1.0 churn on these enums, this is the highest-value missing coverage in the SPI command path.
findings.recommendation: Add a Tests/unit suite mocking KNS_Q_pop and USERDATA_txFifo* to drive macEvtProcess through each event id and assert macStatus + cbStatus + whether txFifoRemoveElt was called, including the empty-FIFO case. Also cover process_cmd bounds (cmd==0, cmd==SPICMD_MAX_COUNT, NULL handler).

dead_code: macStatusAcknowledged (52-57, 352/363/377/388): genuine orphan write-only flag — assigned here and in two sibling files but never read as a condition anywhere in the tree; the latch it documents is unimplemented (see finding). The DEBUG trace block (71-78) is config-gated (compiled only when DEBUG defined) — intentional. KNS_MAC_ERROR appears in both switches (327-334 setup, then 424-430 status) — both reachable, not dead. The whole file is dead in the sealed UART deployment but live for COMM=SPI (config-gated, intentional). No unreachable branches in the dispatch.
test_coverage: Testable logic (macEvtProcess event mapping, process_cmd dispatch bounds, process_transaction A+/legacy routing) is NOT covered. Tests/unit/test_spi_protocol.c exercises only the protocol layer (mgr_spi_protocol.c CRC/framing) with zero references to this file's functions. Concrete gaps: the event->MACStatus switch and the empty-FIFO NULL path. HW glue (DMA arming) is not unit-testable, but the pure mapping logic is and should be mocked.

role: SPI-host command helpers: maps app error codes to protocol status, builds A+/legacy error responses, and wraps handler payloads into A+ protocol response frames for the pipelined SPI slave protocol.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only (Makefile:412-420 gates the whole MGR_SPI_CMD dir on USE_SPI_DRIVER). Sealed deployment target is COMM=UART, so this file is NOT compiled in the sealed config; it is live only for the SPI host (e.g. GUI/external-MCU) build.

findings.description: Payload/frame size limits are inconsistent across the SPI send path. bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread clamps payload_len to SPI_FRAME_MAX_DATA (250) and builds an A+ frame of up to 4+250+1 = 255 bytes into txBuf.data, setting txBuf.next_req = frame_len. But the actual transmit path MCU_SPI_DRIVER_set_response() (called by the caller MGR_SPI_CMD_process_cmd at mgr_spi_cmd.c:95) hard-rejects any len > SPI_TRANSACTION_SIZE (64), returning false WITHOUT setting any response. The transaction is also a fixed 64 bytes (SPI_TRANSACTION_SIZE). So any A+ response whose total frame exceeds 64 bytes (payload > ~59 bytes) is built successfully here, passes this file's 250-byte validation, then is silently dropped at send time.
findings.impact: For the SPI host build, large A+ responses (e.g. previpass/long status payloads) are never transmitted. The master polls and receives only the idle pattern (0xAA) for the prior command, with no error frame back. Depending on master firmware this manifests as a hang/timeout or infinite retry on that command. Not in the sealed UART deployment, but a real protocol break for the SPI/GUI config.
findings.recommendation: Make the limits agree: clamp/validate against SPI_TRANSACTION_SIZE (64) here (account for 5-byte A+ header+CRC, so payload <= 59), OR raise SPI_TRANSACTION_SIZE / make set_response accept the full frame. At minimum, check the return value of MCU_SPI_DRIVER_set_response and emit an explicit error frame (SPI_PROT_STATUS_SIZE_ERROR) when the response does not fit, so the master never sees a dropped response.

findings.location: mgr_spi_cmd.c:94-96 (set by this file's writeread); mgr_spi_cmd_common.c:151,161-167
findings.description: bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread builds the frame and sets txBuf.next_req but does NOT itself call MCU_SPI_DRIVER_set_response; it relies on the caller (MGR_SPI_CMD_process_cmd) doing so only when ret==true AND txBuf.next_req>0. The function's own trailing comment (lines 161-167) is uncertain and self-contradictory ('we can also call it here to make sure it is set. Actually, the response is already in txBuf...'). Because set_response's failure (the size bug above) is checked only by the caller's ignored bool return, a too-large frame leaves response_ready=false and the previous transaction's stale TX content armed.
findings.impact: Combined with the size mismatch, a failed set_response is swallowed: master receives stale/idle data instead of a defined error. Hard to diagnose in the field on the SPI host link.
findings.recommendation: Centralize response commit in one place and check its return. Either always call MCU_SPI_DRIVER_set_response inside writeread and return its status, or have the caller treat a false return as an error and build an explicit NACK frame. Remove the contradictory comment.

findings.description: bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_read is declared to return uint8_t (header mgr_spi_cmd_common.h:83) but returns HAL_OK (a HAL_StatusTypeDef enum value). It is documented as a near no-op. Type punning HAL_StatusTypeDef into uint8_t is an implicit narrowing cast (MISRA-like concern), and the doxygen comment in the header (says it 'reads data via SPI_Read_IT', 'returns the byte read') no longer matches the pipelined no-op behavior (comment rot).
findings.impact: Cosmetic/maintainability only; HAL_OK==0 fits in uint8_t. The stale doc could mislead a future maintainer into thinking this still performs a read.
findings.recommendation: Return HAL_OK with a matching return type or change the prototype to HAL_StatusTypeDef for consistency with bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread. Update the header doxygen to describe the actual no-op pipelined behavior.

findings.description: Both A+ paths dereference MGR_SPI_PROTOCOL_get_request() (req->sequence) without a NULL check. get_request() currently always returns &spi_protocol_ctx.request so it cannot be NULL in practice, but the A+ branch is entered based on spi_protocol_ctx.mode==SPI_PROTOCOL_A_PLUS which may not be in sync with a freshly parsed request if these helpers are ever called outside the normal process_transaction->process_cmd ordering. The functions trust txBuf.next_req (a global) was correctly set by the handler before being called.
findings.impact: Low given current single-threaded call ordering and non-NULL invariant. Latent fragility if the call sequence changes.
findings.recommendation: Add a defensive assert/early-return that req != NULL, or document the non-NULL invariant inline. No behavioral change needed today.

findings.description: payload_backup[SPI_FRAME_MAX_DATA] is a 250-byte stack buffer copied from txBuf.data and then fed back into MGR_SPI_PROTOCOL_build_response writing into the same txBuf.data. The backup is needed because build_response writes the header in place over the start of the payload, so the copy-out/copy-in is correct (no in-place overlap corruption). The 250-byte stack frame is acceptable for this SPI task context. Bounds are safe: memcpy length is the validated payload_len (<=250) and build_response writes <=255 into txBuf.data (256 bytes).
findings.impact: None — noted to confirm the in-place reframing is safe and bounds hold within txBuf.
findings.recommendation: No change. If stack budget on the SPI build is tight, the backup could be avoided by building the header in a small fixed array and prepending, but not necessary.

findings.description: map_error_to_protocol_status omits ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_AVAILABLE (added in kineis_sw_conf.h:61) and ERROR_UNKNOWN_AT_CMD is mapped but the broad default catches the rest. ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_AVAILABLE falls through default to SPI_PROT_STATUS_ERROR (generic) rather than a more specific INVALID_CMD/NOT_READY. Switch has no missing-break defects; default is explicit.
findings.impact: Minor: SPI host sees generic ERROR (0x01) for feature-not-available instead of a distinct code; the detailed app error code is still in the A+ payload bytes so the master can disambiguate. Pure quality nit.
findings.recommendation: Optionally add a case for ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_AVAILABLE (e.g. SPI_PROT_STATUS_INVALID_CMD) for clearer host-side handling. Not required.

dead_code: No genuine orphans inside the file. All three public functions are called from the SPI command handlers (mgr_spi_cmd_list_*.c) and map_error_to_protocol_status is used locally. The ENTIRE file, however, is config-gated dead code in the sealed deployment: it is compiled only when COMM=SPI (Makefile:412-420 / USE_SPI_DRIVER), and the sealed target builds COMM=UART. So for the epoxy-sealed UW_DOPPLER/SMD_STDALONE/UART unit none of this code is reachable. It is intentional config gating, not an orphan — it serves the SPI host (GUI/external-MCU) build.
test_coverage: No unit test in Tests/unit references writeread, logFailedMsg, map_error_to_protocol_status, or build_response (grep over Tests/ returned nothing). Concrete gaps worth covering on the SPI build: (1) the size-limit boundary — a response whose A+ frame exceeds SPI_TRANSACTION_SIZE (64) should produce a defined error, not a silent drop (the high finding); (2) map_error_to_protocol_status mapping table (each ERROR_RETURN_T -> expected SpiProtocolStatus, including the default and the unmapped ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_AVAILABLE); (3) error-code 2-byte big-endian encoding for values >255 (e.g. ERROR_PARAMETER_FORMAT=1200 -> 0x04,0xB0). These are pure-logic functions that mock cleanly (MGR_SPI_PROTOCOL_build_response + a stub txBuf), so they are good unit-test candidates even though the file is not in the sealed config.

role: Defines the SPI command dispatch table cas_spicmd_list_array[0x40] (command-byte -> handler fn) and the spicmd_version string. Pure data file; consumed by mgr_spi_cmd.c which indexes the array by the raw incoming command byte.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only (Makefile:412-427 gate the whole MGR_SPI_CMD/*.c under `ifeq ($(COMM),SPI)`). NOT compiled for the sealed deployment target (APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART, per Makefile:992-993). So in the sealed UART build this file and table are entirely absent.

findings.description: The dispatcher indexes cas_spicmd_list_array[cmd] directly by the raw command byte (mgr_spi_cmd.c:90-91) and never validates that row .cmd equals its array index. The table is therefore a positional contract: row N MUST have .cmd == N. I verified the current 64 rows are all correctly aligned (0x00..0x2A sequential, 0x2B=CMD_READ_RCONF_RAW, 0x2C..0x3E=CMD_NONE filler, 0x3F=CMD_DFU_ENTER). But there is no _Static_assert or runtime guard tying index to .cmd. Inserting, deleting or reordering a single row (e.g. adding a new mid-range command) silently shifts every subsequent handler by one slot, so an incoming command would invoke the WRONG handler with no error.
findings.impact: Latent landmine. A future edit to this list could map e.g. CMD_WRITE_SECKEY's byte onto CMD_WRITE_TX's handler, or a benign read onto bMGR_SPI_CMD_DFU_ENTER_cmd (which resets to bootloader). Silent mis-dispatch, hard to catch without a host-side functional test. No impact on the sealed UART deployment (file not compiled there).
findings.recommendation: Add a build-time guard: either a `_Static_assert(SPICMD_MAX_COUNT == 0x40, ...)` plus a one-time init/test loop asserting `cas_spicmd_list_array[i].cmd == i || cas_spicmd_list_array[i].cmd == CMD_NONE` for all i, or have the dispatcher check `cas_spicmd_list_array[cmd].cmd == cmd` before calling. A Tests/unit case is the cheapest guard.

findings.description: The struct field .next_cmd is populated on ~12 rows (e.g. line 39 CMD_WRITE_RCONF, line 48 CMD_WRITE_TX_SIZE) but is NEVER read anywhere in MGR_SPI_CMD (grep confirms only .f_ht_cmd_fun_proc is referenced, mgr_spi_cmd.c:90-91). The pipelined SPI protocol does not use a next-command state machine; the _REQ->value handshake is handled inside the handler functions via userTxPayloadSize and similar. next_cmd is a vestige carried over from the AT-command-manager twin design.
findings.impact: No functional impact (config-gated file, dead field). Wastes a little flash (one CmdValue per row) and misleads a reader into thinking a two-step handshake is enforced by the table when it is not.
findings.recommendation: Either remove the next_cmd field from struct spicmd_desc_t and the table, or document at the struct decl that it is reserved/unused by the SPI dispatcher. Low priority.

findings.description: The .cmd field (first column) is also never read at runtime by the dispatcher (it trusts the array index instead). It is purely decorative documentation. Combined with finding #1, this means the table carries an apparent self-describing key (.cmd) that the runtime ignores, increasing the risk that a maintainer trusts the .cmd values rather than the row order.
findings.impact: Documentation/maintainability hazard, not a runtime defect. Reinforces the positional-fragility risk of finding #1.
findings.recommendation: Make .cmd load-bearing by validating it against the index at init/test time (see #1 recommendation), turning a decorative field into an actual integrity check.

findings.description: File-header Doxygen says `@file mgr_at_cmd_list.c` but the file is mgr_spi_cmd_list.c. Copy-paste rot from the AT-command twin. Similarly the struct doc in mgr_spi_cmd_list.h:123 describes commands as 'SPI+XXXX=...' / 'SPI+XXXX=?' (an AT-string format) whereas this is a binary command-byte protocol.
findings.impact: Cosmetic. Misleads Doxygen output and readers; no runtime effect.
findings.recommendation: Fix @file to mgr_spi_cmd_list.c and drop/correct the 'SPI+XXXX=...' description in the struct doc.

findings.description: No unit test references cas_spicmd_list_array, spicmd_version, or SPICMD_MAX_COUNT (grep over Tests/ returns nothing). The single most valuable, cheapest test for this file — assert that for every i in [0,SPICMD_MAX_COUNT), the row's .cmd is either i or CMD_NONE, and that DFU_ENTER sits exactly at 0x3F — does not exist. This is the guard that would catch the finding #1 misalignment automatically.
findings.impact: A reordering/insertion bug (finding #1) would not be caught by CI; it would only surface as wrong-handler behaviour on a live SPI host bench.
findings.recommendation: Add Tests/unit case: loop the table asserting index/.cmd alignment, count==0x40, all listed handlers non-NULL where .cmd!=CMD_NONE, and all CMD_NONE rows have NULL handler.

findings.description: Entire file is config-gated dead code for the sealed deployment: Makefile:412-427 compiles MGR_SPI_CMD/*.c only under COMM=SPI, and the sealed target is COMM=UART (Makefile:992-993). This is intentional (GUI/SPI-host builds use it), not an orphan. Noted so reviewers don't treat any finding here as a sealed-deploy brick path — none of these reach the UART firmware.
findings.impact: None on sealed UART deployment. Relevant only to COMM=SPI builds (GUI/host-driven).
findings.recommendation: No action; documenting reachability boundary.

dead_code: Whole file: config-gated dead in the sealed deployment (COMM=UART) — only compiled when COMM=SPI (Makefile:412-427); intentional, not an orphan. Within the file: (1) .next_cmd column (mgr_spi_cmd_list.c table + .h:127) is genuinely dead — never read by any caller (only .f_ht_cmd_fun_proc is dereferenced at mgr_spi_cmd.c:90-91). (2) .cmd column is effectively dead at runtime (decorative; dispatcher uses the array index, not this field). (3) Rows 0x2C..0x3E are intentional NULL-handler filler reserving the DFU/bootloader range; reachable as commands but route to the NULL-handler path (ret=false, logged) — correct defensive behaviour, not dead. No unreachable branches (it is a data file, no control flow).
test_coverage: No coverage. Zero Tests/unit references to cas_spicmd_list_array / spicmd_version / SPICMD_MAX_COUNT. The table is pure data but its correctness is entirely positional and unguarded, so it is exactly the kind of thing a unit test should pin: (a) index==.cmd (or CMD_NONE) for all 0x40 rows, (b) row count == SPICMD_MAX_COUNT, (c) CMD_DFU_ENTER at 0x3F, (d) every non-CMD_NONE row has a non-NULL handler and every CMD_NONE row has NULL. None of these invariants are tested. Concrete gap, easy to fill.

role: SPI command handlers for certification CW (Continuous Wave) read/write commands (CMD_READ_CW/WRITE_CW_REQ/WRITE_CW). Per the header/enum these are unimplemented stubs that just emit a 1-byte 0x00 response.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only (Makefile:412-428 gates all MGR_SPI_CMD/*.c under ifeq($(COMM),SPI)). The sealed deployment target is APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART, so this file is NOT compiled into the sealed image. It is live only on SPI-host builds.

findings.description: The `if (ret == HAL_OK) return true; else return false;` branch's false-arm is unreachable. `bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread()` (mgr_spi_cmd_common.c:114-168) has no failure path and unconditionally `return HAL_OK;` (line 167). Therefore `ret` is always HAL_OK and these handlers can never return false. The whole construct is equivalent to `return true;`.
findings.impact: No functional harm, but it gives the dispatcher (mgr_spi_cmd.c:91-96) the false impression that a failure is possible/handled. Dead error-handling masks the fact that there is no real error checking. Not in the sealed image.
findings.recommendation: Replace the three-function body with a single `return (bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread() == HAL_OK);` or just `return true;`, and document that the underlying call cannot fail.

findings.description: Every handler logs `"[ERROR] Status mode is unauthorized for this AT cmd\r\n"` unconditionally on entry, then proceeds to build a normal success response (`tx->data[0]=0; next_req=1`) and returns true. The log message is factually wrong: there is no status-mode check, nothing is rejected, and the command 'succeeds'. The text was evidently copy-pasted from a real authorization-guarded handler.
findings.impact: Comment/log rot. On a SPI-host build with VERBOSE logging, the host operator sees a spurious '[ERROR] ... unauthorized' line for a command that actually returned OK, which will mislead field/cert debugging. No effect on sealed (UART) deployment.
findings.recommendation: Remove the misleading log line or replace with an honest message such as `"[STUB] READCW/WRITECW not implemented\r\n"`. Align all three.

findings.description: These are stubs (file header line 7 and enum comments mgr_spi_cmd_list.h:76-78 both say 'not implemented'), yet they return success (true) and emit a 1-byte 0x00 payload rather than signalling 'unimplemented/invalid' to the host. The dispatcher only NACKs when the handler returns false or next_req==0 (mgr_spi_cmd.c:90-100). A host issuing CMD_READ_CW/WRITE_CW gets a positive ACK with a meaningless 0x00 byte and no way to detect the feature is absent.
findings.impact: Silent wrong-result: a certification host cannot distinguish 'CW read returned 0' from 'CW not implemented'. Cert tooling could misinterpret a stub as a valid CW reading. SPI-host builds only; not in sealed image.
findings.recommendation: Either implement, or have the stubs return false (so the dispatcher NACKs) / set an explicit not-supported status. Decide the host contract explicitly.

findings.description: The `rx` parameter is never read in any of the three handlers (they only write to `tx` and set `rx->next_req=1`). The CW write handlers in particular ignore the incoming payload entirely, consistent with them being stubs.
findings.impact: None functionally; flags that the 'write' handlers discard host input. Could trip -Wunused-parameter only if rx were truly untouched (it is touched via rx->next_req), so no warning. Documentation/intent gap only.
findings.recommendation: No action beyond the stub-contract decision above; when implemented, the write handlers must consume rx->data.

findings.description: `uint8_t ret = HAL_OK;` stores the result of `bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread()` (declared `uint8_t`, returns the HAL_StatusTypeDef value HAL_OK=0) into a uint8_t and compares against HAL_OK. Mixing HAL_StatusTypeDef with a bool-named `b...` function and a uint8_t holder is a minor type/naming inconsistency (the function is prefixed `b` implying bool but returns uint8_t). No defect today since HAL_OK fits in uint8_t.
findings.impact: Cosmetic / maintainability. If the driver were ever changed to return a wider/negative status, the uint8_t truncation could silently lose information.
findings.recommendation: Use the actual return type (HAL_StatusTypeDef) or bool consistently; rename `b...` if it does not return bool.

dead_code: The entire file is config-gated dead code for the sealed deployment: compiled only under COMM=SPI (Makefile:412-428); the sealed target is COMM=UART, so none of it ships in the epoxy-sealed image. Within the file, the `else { return false; }` arms (lines 42-44, 64-66, 86-88) are genuinely unreachable in ALL configs because the called function cannot return non-HAL_OK. The three functions themselves are live (registered in cas_spicmd_list_array at mgr_spi_cmd_list.c:51-53) on SPI builds, so they are not orphans — just stubs.
test_coverage: No unit test references these handlers or the CMD_READ_CW/CMD_WRITE_CW commands (grep of Tests/** for READCW/WRITECW/CMD_*_CW returned nothing). Testable logic is minimal (stubs), but a small test asserting the dispatcher's contract for stub commands (return value + 1-byte response, or that they correctly NACK once a real contract is chosen) would lock down behavior and catch the always-true return. Low priority since the file is not in the sealed (UART) build.

role: SPI command handlers for general device management (ID/ADDR/SN/seckey/RCONF/LPM/TCXO read-write, DFU entry) over the pipelined single-transaction SPI protocol; host-controlled (GUI master), not the sealed UART path.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only. The whole file is added to C_SOURCES under `ifeq ($(COMM),SPI)` (Makefile:412-424) and every handler body is implicitly guarded by USE_SPI_DRIVER via the SPI_Buffer type. NOT built for the sealed deployment (APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART), whose default is COMM=UART (Makefile:94). Live in GUI/host configs built with COMM=SPI.
dead_code: Entire file is dead in the sealed-deploy target (COMM=UART) — intentional, config-gated by the Makefile, not an orphan. Within a COMM=SPI build all 30 handlers are reachable via cas_spicmd_list_array[] (mgr_spi_cmd_list.c:26-94) dispatched from MGR_SPI_CMD_process_cmd (mgr_spi_cmd.c:90-91). Constants CMD_WRITELPM_WAIT_LEN (mgr_spi_cmd_list.h:40) and CMD_WRITETCXO_WAIT_LEN (line 36) are defined but never referenced in this file — genuine orphan macros (the analogous WAIT_LEN guards ARE used for WRITEID/WRITEADDRESS/WRITESECKEY/WRITERCONF but the LPM and TCXO handlers skip them). When DEBUG=0, sec_key_str (line 315-319) and rconf_str (line 566-570) plus their sprintf loops are dead computation: their only consumer is MGR_LOG_DEBUG which expands to do{}while(0) (mgr_log.h:88).

findings.description: The entire translation unit is compiled only when COMM=SPI. The sealed deployment target is COMM=UART, so none of these handlers ship in the sealed firmware.
findings.impact: Greatly reduces the brick/hang/corrupt risk of this file for the sealed ocean deployment: the SPI command path is simply absent. All findings below apply to GUI/host-controlled COMM=SPI builds only.
findings.recommendation: No action; documented so reviewers do not over-weight SPI findings against the sealed target. If a COMM=SPI variant is ever sealed, re-triage the medium findings as deployment-relevant.

findings.description: Reads rx->data[1] (the LPM bitmap) with no length check. Unlike WRITEID/WRITEADDRESS/WRITESECKEY/WRITERCONF, this handler never validates rx->size against CMD_WRITELPM_WAIT_LEN (=2, defined but unused). A frame carrying only the command byte (rx->size==1, e.g. SPI desync / truncated A+ frame) makes data[1] a stale leftover from a previous transaction's rxBuf, which is then written into lpm_config.allowedLPMbitmap.
findings.impact: A corrupted/short frame can silently reprogram the allowed-LPM bitmap. If the stale byte masks off all sleep modes (bitmap=NONE) the device stops entering low power (battery drain); if it forces an unintended deep mode it changes wake behavior. No OOB read (rxBuf.data is 256 bytes), so memory-safe, but the policy write is unvalidated.
findings.recommendation: Mirror the other writers: `if (rx->size < CMD_WRITELPM_WAIT_LEN) return bMGR_SPI_CMD_logFailedMsg(ERROR_MISSING_PARAMETERS, tx);` before reading data[1]. This also makes the orphan CMD_WRITELPM_WAIT_LEN macro live.

findings.description: memcpy(&tcxo_ms, &rx->data[1], 4) with no length check. CMD_WRITETCXO_WAIT_LEN (=5) is defined but unused here, whereas the structurally identical WRITEID handler DOES guard with CMD_WRITEID_WAIT_LEN (line 435). A short frame copies up to 3 stale bytes from rxBuf into tcxo_ms.
findings.impact: A truncated frame can set an arbitrary (stale) TCXO warmup value, capped only by the 0..30000 ms range check. A wrong warmup shifts RF timing/power but cannot brick; no OOB (256-byte buffer). Memory-safe but value is unvalidated for completeness.
findings.recommendation: Add `if (rx->size < CMD_WRITETCXO_WAIT_LEN) return bMGR_SPI_CMD_logFailedMsg(ERROR_MISSING_PARAMETERS, tx);` before the memcpy, matching WRITEID.

findings.location: mgr_spi_cmd_common.h:93 vs mcu_spi_driver.h:167 (use sites e.g. mgr_spi_cmd_list_general.c:57-61)
findings.description: bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread() is prototyped as returning uint8_t, but it is #defined to MCU_SPI_DRIVER_read which returns HAL_StatusTypeDef. Most handlers store the result in `HAL_StatusTypeDef ret`, while bMGR_SPI_CMD_READ_cmd (line 57) uses `uint8_t ret = HAL_OK`. The prototype is never actually the called symbol (the macro wins), so the declared return type is misleading.
findings.impact: Works today only because HAL_OK==0 and HAL_StatusTypeDef fits in uint8_t. A future HAL status value >255 or a reviewer trusting the uint8_t prototype could be misled. No runtime defect now.
findings.recommendation: Fix the prototype to return HAL_StatusTypeDef (or document the macro override), and make the local `ret` type consistent across handlers.

findings.description: HAL_Delay(100) is a blocking busy-wait in the main-loop command handler, used to let the master clock out the ACK before request_dfu_mode() resets the chip.
findings.impact: Stalls the cooperative main loop for 100 ms (no MAC/LPM servicing during that window). Acceptable because a system reset follows immediately, but it is a hard busy-wait on the only thread.
findings.recommendation: Keep, but note the dependency: this assumes the SPI master polls the response within 100 ms. If that assumption ever changes, prefer arming the response then resetting on the next transaction rather than a fixed delay.

findings.description: READRCONF returns the decoded in-memory `struct KNS_CFG_radio_t` raw over SPI (memcpy of the struct incl. int8_t+3 padding bytes, enum width, host endianness), whereas WRITERCONF and READRCONFRAW operate on the raw 16-byte encrypted block. Read and write are therefore asymmetric and the read exposes implementation-defined struct padding.
findings.impact: A master cannot round-trip READRCONF->WRITERCONF (different formats), and the padding bytes are indeterminate stack content sent on the wire (minor info leak / non-portable). Not a memory-safety bug; sizeof(struct)=16 fits the 256-byte buffer and the <59-byte transaction limit.
findings.recommendation: Document the format difference, or have READRCONF return the same raw 16-byte block as READRCONFRAW for symmetry. At minimum zero-init the struct so padding is deterministic.

findings.description: The anti-garbage guards reject ID==0x00000000 / 0xFFFFFFFF and ADDR/SECKEY/RCONF that are all-zero or all-0xFF as 'SPI desync'. These are heuristics: a legitimately all-0xFF or all-zero value is refused.
findings.impact: Provisioning a (admittedly unlikely) all-0xFF/all-zero ADDR/ID/SECKEY/RCONF is impossible via SPI. Defensive-by-design and low probability, but it is a hard policy embedded in the data-plane.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable as a desync filter; just confirm Kineis never issues such boundary credential values. No code change required.

findings.description: sec_key_str holds the 16-byte AES device secret key as a 32-char hex string on the stack, built solely to feed MGR_LOG_DEBUG. With DEBUG=0 the sprintf loop runs but its only consumer compiles out (dead work); with DEBUG=1 the plaintext key is printed to the console.
findings.impact: DEBUG=1: secret key material is emitted in cleartext on the UART log (forensic/security exposure). Any build: the key copy lingers in stack memory after return. Low severity (host-side, COMM=SPI, debug-gated) but it is sensitive data.
findings.recommendation: Do not log the full key (log a hash/prefix or nothing). Consider explicit_bzero of sec_key_str before return so key material does not persist on the stack.

findings.description: No unit test exercises any handler in this file. The existing Tests/unit/test_spi_protocol.c covers only the bootloader DFU frame protocol, not these command handlers' validation logic.
findings.impact: The size/garbage-validation branches (the most defect-prone part: WRITEID/ADDR/SECKEY/RCONF guards, the missing LPM/TCXO guards, the macStatus terminal-status latch in READSPIMACSTATE) are untested. Regressions in validation would ship unnoticed in COMM=SPI builds.
findings.recommendation: Add a unit test mocking SPI_Buffer + MCU_NVM_*/KNS_CFG_* that feeds short/garbage/valid frames to WRITEID/WRITEADDRESS/WRITESECKEY/WRITERCONF/WRITELPM/WRITETCXO and asserts the correct error code or accepted value, plus a READSPIMACSTATE test covering the terminal-vs-non-terminal reset branches.

test_coverage: No coverage. The pure, testable logic (frame size validation, all-zero/all-0xFF garbage detection, LPM bitmap masking at line 666, TCXO range check at line 741, READSPIMACSTATE terminal-status latch at lines 360-377) has no unit test in Tests/unit. test_spi_protocol.c tests a different layer (bootloader DFU framing). Concrete gaps: the missing-guard paths in WRITELPM/WRITETCXO and the validation branches in WRITEID/ADDR/SECKEY/RCONF. The thin handlers (READ/PING/SPISTATE etc.) are HW glue and need only minimal coverage.

role: SPI-console command handlers for the Kineis MAC subset (READKMAC / WRITEKMACREQ / WRITEKMAC): reads current MAC profile info and pushes a MAC-init event onto the APP2MAC queue on behalf of the GUI.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only (Makefile line 425, inside the `ifeq ($(COMM),SPI)` block). NOT compiled for the sealed deployment (APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART). Header file note "actually stubs ... only present because GUI is sending such AT commands" — these are GUI-facing SPI handlers.

findings.description: Stack buffer over-read in bMGR_SPI_CMD_READKMAC_cmd. `prfl_info.id` is `enum KNS_MAC_prflId_t` which is a 4-byte int (no -fshort-enums in Makefile; only -mcpu=cortex-m4 -mthumb at Makefile:269/278). The packed struct (kns_mac_prfl_cfg.h:96-103) is sizeof = 4 (id) + 11 (largest union member SATDET = 1+1+1+4+4) = 15 bytes. The code does `prflCfgPtr = &prfl_info.prflCfgPtr` (union start, offset 4) then `memcpy(&tx->data[1], prflCfgPtr, sizeof(prfl_info) - 1)` = copies 14 bytes from offset 4. Only 11 bytes of struct remain past offset 4 (offsets 4..14), so it reads offsets 15,16,17 — 3 bytes PAST the end of the 15-byte stack struct. The `-1` is hard-coded on the false assumption that `id` is 1 byte.
findings.impact: Reads 3 bytes of uninitialized adjacent stack and ships them to the SPI master as part of the profile config. UB / information leak of stack contents; the returned profile config bytes are also misaligned (the upper 3 zero bytes of the 4-byte id are skipped, so id is sent as 1 byte but the union starts at tx->data[1] correctly only by coincidence on little-endian). Not in the sealed UART build, but corrupts/leaks for any COMM=SPI GUI build.
findings.recommendation: Copy exactly the union size, not `sizeof(prfl_info)-1`. e.g. `memcpy(&tx->data[1], &prfl_info.prflCfgPtr, sizeof(prfl_info) - sizeof(prfl_info.id))` (= 11), and set `tx->next_req` to 1 + that value. Add a `_Static_assert` pinning the expected struct size so a libkineis layout change can't silently re-introduce the over-read.

findings.description: Return value of `KNS_MAC_getPrflInfo(&prfl_info)` (declared `enum KNS_status_t KNS_MAC_getPrflInfo(...)` in kns_mac.h:100) is ignored. `prfl_info` is an uninitialized stack struct; if the MAC call fails and does not fully populate it, the handler still copies and transmits whatever is on the stack.
findings.impact: On a failed/partial MAC query the SPI master receives garbage profile data with a success framing, with no error indication. COMM=SPI only.
findings.recommendation: Check the status; on != KNS_STATUS_OK return bMGR_SPI_CMD_logFailedMsg(ERROR_UNKNOWN, tx). Optionally zero-init prfl_info.

findings.description: `appEvt.init_prfl_ctxt.id = rx->data[1];` takes an attacker/GUI-controlled byte and assigns it directly to the MAC profile id enum with no range check against KNS_MAC_PRFL_MAX (kns_mac_prfl_cfg.h:56). The value is then pushed into the MAC via KNS_Q_push and consumed by closed-source libkineis. Also rx->data[1] is read with no check that the received frame actually contained >= 2 bytes (no data_len validation in this handler).
findings.impact: An out-of-range profile id (e.g. >= KNS_MAC_PRFL_MAX, or a stale rx->data[1] if the frame was short) is handed to the trusted MAC boundary. Behavior of libkineis on an invalid profile id is unknown; could mis-init the MAC. COMM=SPI only, but the GUI write path is reachable.
findings.recommendation: Validate `rx->data[1] < KNS_MAC_PRFL_MAX` (and that the request carried the id byte) before assigning; reject with bMGR_SPI_CMD_logFailedMsg(ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_VALUE, tx) otherwise.

findings.description: Entire translation unit is config-gated dead code for the sealed target: compiled only under `ifeq ($(COMM),SPI)` (Makefile:412-428, file at :425). The sealed deployment is COMM=UART (Makefile:94 default, and the documented bench/release lines Makefile:992-993 use COMM=UART), where this file is not built. Intentional, not an orphan — it is the SPI counterpart of the UART AT-command MAC handlers. Note also the file/header banner still says `@file mgr_at_cmd_list_mac.c` / `@author Kinéis` (comment rot from a copy of the AT version).
findings.impact: No impact on the sealed UART build. Listed for reachability clarity: the bugs above only affect COMM=SPI (GUI/STDLN-over-SPI) builds.
findings.recommendation: No action for the seal. If desired, fix the stale `@file`/`@author` doxygen banner (says mgr_at_cmd_list_mac.c) to mgr_spi_cmd_list_mac.c.

findings.description: Repeated `HAL_StatusTypeDef ret = ...; if (ret==HAL_OK) return true; else return false;` boilerplate is just `return (bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread() == HAL_OK);`. Note bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread() actually returns uint8_t (mgr_spi_cmd_common.c:114), not HAL_StatusTypeDef, so the local `ret` type is an implicit-cast mismatch with the declared type — works only because HAL_OK==0.
findings.impact: Cosmetic / minor MISRA implicit-type concern. No functional defect.
findings.recommendation: Collapse to a single return and use the actual return type (uint8_t) or a bool, consistently across the three handlers.

findings.description: The switch on KNS_Q_push status handles KNS_STATUS_QFULL and KNS_STATUS_OK; default maps everything else to ERROR_UNKNOWN. Each case ends with both `break;` after a `return` (unreachable break after return) and an empty OK case followed by break — harmless but the `break` statements after `return` are dead.
findings.impact: None functional; minor dead statements / style.
findings.recommendation: Drop the redundant `break;` after `return` and the empty OK case fallthrough; keep the default error mapping.

dead_code: Whole file is config-gated (compiled only for COMM=SPI; Makefile:425 inside the SPI ifeq). It is the SPI sibling of the UART AT MAC handlers, intentionally excluded from the COMM=UART sealed build — not a genuine orphan. Within the functions: the `break;` statements at lines 88/90/93 are unreachable (each case returns first) — dead but harmless. No unused statics; `(void)rx` casts at lines 34/55 are intentional unused-param suppression (note rx IS used in WRITEKMAC at line 82, correctly not cast there).
test_coverage: No unit test covers these handlers. Tests/unit has test_spi_protocol.c (frame/CRC layer) and test_state_machine.c, but neither exercises bMGR_SPI_CMD_READKMAC/WRITEKMACREQ/WRITEKMAC. Concrete gaps: (1) a host test pinning sizeof(struct KNS_MAC_prflInfo_t)==15 and verifying READKMAC copies exactly the union (11 bytes) into tx->data[1..] with no over-read (catch the line 42 bug); (2) WRITEKMAC range-rejecting rx->data[1] >= KNS_MAC_PRFL_MAX and short-frame cases; (3) WRITEKMAC mapping KNS_STATUS_QFULL -> ERROR_DATA_QUEUE_FULL. Mock KNS_MAC_getPrflInfo / KNS_Q_push as the framework already mocks MGR_*/HAL_*. Currently this is HW/GUI glue with real testable logic that is untested.

role: Six stub SPI-command handlers for PREPASSEN (0x1A-0x1C) and UDATE (0x1D-0x1F); each just emits a 1-byte 0x00 response. Exists only so the GUI's SPI command set is acknowledged, not implemented.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only. Gated by the ifeq($(COMM),SPI) block in Makefile (lines 412-428, file at line 427) and by #ifdef USE_SPI_DRIVER in mcu_spi_driver.h which is the only place SPI_Buffer / bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread exist. NEVER compiled in the sealed deployment (APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART). All callers are the dispatch table cas_spicmd_list_array[] in mgr_spi_cmd_list.c, invoked via MGR_SPI_CMD_process_cmd -> f_ht_cmd_fun_proc(&rxBuf,&txBuf).

findings.description: Entire translation unit is config-gated: it compiles and links ONLY when COMM=SPI (Makefile:412-428, file listed at line 427; types/symbols guarded by #ifdef USE_SPI_DRIVER in mcu_spi_driver.h:35). The sealed deployment target is COMM=UART, so none of this code is in the sealed binary.
findings.impact: No runtime impact on the sealed (UART) build - it is entirely absent. Relevant only if a COMM=SPI variant is ever shipped. Flagged as intentional config-gating, not an orphan.
findings.recommendation: No action for the sealed build. Keep aware that audit findings below only matter for a hypothetical COMM=SPI release.

findings.description: The `else { return false; }` branch is unreachable in all six functions. `ret` is assigned from bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread(), which (mgr_spi_cmd_common.c:114-168) unconditionally `return HAL_OK;` on every path. HAL_OK==0, so `ret == HAL_OK` is always true and the false branch is genuine dead code. Also `ret` is pre-initialised to HAL_OK at declaration (e.g. line 34) then immediately overwritten - the init is redundant.
findings.impact: Misleading error-handling shape: the code looks like it checks for an SPI failure, but bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread can never report one, so a real failure to build/queue the response would be silently reported as success (true). Low impact because the payload is a fixed 1-byte stub, but the pattern hides the fact that the SPI layer gives no usable error feedback here.
findings.recommendation: Either make bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread return a meaningful status, or drop the dead branch and just `return true;`. At minimum remove the redundant `= HAL_OK` initialiser.

findings.description: Comment-rot / misleading log: every stub logs `"[ERROR] Status mode is unauthorized for this AT cmd"`. These are not error paths and the command is not unauthorised - they are intentional no-op stubs that return a normal OK response (tx->data[0]=0, next_req=1, function returns true). The message is copy-pasted and contradicts the actual behaviour. The string is only compiled when DEBUG=1 and VERBOSE is defined (mgr_log.h:75/81/90: MGR_LOG_VERBOSE is a no-op otherwise), so it costs nothing in release, but on a VERBOSE SPI bench build it would spam false '[ERROR]' lines for normal PREPASSEN/UDATE polling.
findings.impact: Operator confusion during SPI bench debugging: legitimate GUI polling of prepass/date would print '[ERROR] ... unauthorized' while the device actually answers OK. No functional effect.
findings.recommendation: Change the text to reflect reality, e.g. "[STUB] PREPASSEN/UDATE not implemented, returning 0", or drop the log. Use MGR_LOG_TRACE (severity-named, works in both builds) if any trace is wanted.

findings.description: The `rx` parameter is unused in all six handlers (read handlers never read it; write handlers discard the written value - they are stubs that do not persist prepass-enable or user-date). This is consistent with the stub intent but the parameter generates no -Wunused warning only because it is named and passed by the table signature.
findings.impact: None functional. A reader may assume AT+UDATE actually sets the RTC/date over SPI - it does not. If GUI relies on UDATE to set time for prepass scheduling, that data is silently dropped (but prepass itself is also unimplemented, so internally consistent).
findings.recommendation: Acceptable for a stub. If real UDATE/prepass support is ever needed on SPI, these are the insertion points. Otherwise add a one-line note in the file header that writes are intentionally discarded.

findings.description: Doc comments are wrong/duplicated: bMGR_SPI_CMD_READUDATE, WRITEUDATEREQ and WRITEUDATE all carry the identical Doxygen line 'Process AT command "AT+UDATE" get/set the current user date and UTC time.', and PREPASSEN handlers have empty @brief bodies (lines 26-30, 48-52, 70-74). The header mgr_spi_cmd_list_previpass.h has accurate per-function docs, so the .c comments are redundant and partly misleading (these are SPI handlers, not AT-command handlers).
findings.impact: Documentation only.
findings.recommendation: Remove the stale .c-side @brief lines or align them with the header.

findings.description: No unit test exercises these six handlers (grep over Tests/ for PREPASSEN/UDATE/previpass = 0 hits). The logic is trivial (fixed 1-byte response) and the module is not in the sealed build, so the gap is low value.
findings.impact: If a COMM=SPI build is ever released, a regression that breaks the stub contract (e.g. wrong next_req, NULL handler) would not be caught by CI. Negligible for the current UART-only sealed target.
findings.recommendation: Optional: add a small unit test that calls each handler with a mocked txBuf and asserts next_req==1 and tx->data[0]==0 and return==true, only if SPI is ever productised.

dead_code: Two layers. (1) Whole file is config-gated dead code for the sealed deployment: only built under COMM=SPI (Makefile:412-428). Intentional, not an orphan - the 6 functions ARE referenced by the dispatch table cas_spicmd_list_array[] in mgr_spi_cmd_list.c:54-59. (2) Within each function, the `else { return false; }` branch (lines 43-45, 65-67, 87-89, 108-110, 129-131, 149-151) is unreachable because bMGR_SPI_DRIVER_writeread() always returns HAL_OK (mgr_spi_cmd_common.c:114-168). The `uint8_t ret = HAL_OK;` initialiser is redundant (immediately overwritten). No unused statics (none declared); `rx` param unused in all six (stub by design).
test_coverage: n/a for sealed build (file not compiled under COMM=UART). For COMM=SPI: testable logic is trivial (fixed 1-byte stub response) and currently has zero unit-test coverage in Tests/unit (no PREPASSEN/UDATE/previpass references). Low-value gap given the file is absent from the sealed target.

role: SPI command handlers for the user-data/TX path: set TX size, write raw TX payload, push a KNS_MAC_SEND_DATA event to the MAC queue, plus an (unused) ASCII-hex-to-binary converter.
compiled_in: COMM=SPI only (Makefile line 412-428, inside `ifeq ($(COMM),SPI)`). NOT compiled for the sealed deployment target (APP=UW_DOPPLER BOARD=SMD_STDALONE COMM=UART; COMM defaults to UART at Makefile:94, sealed cmdlines use COMM=UART at Makefile:992-993). Independent of APP/BOARD: any SPI build pulls it in.

findings.description: u16MGR_SPI_CMD_convertAsciiBinary() is a genuine orphan: defined + exported in the header but has zero callers anywhere in the tree (grep across repo finds only the prototype and the definition). The SPI WRITETX path transmits RAW bytes (rx->data copied verbatim, line 235-237), so no ASCII-hex conversion is ever invoked. It has external linkage so the linker cannot dead-strip it; it is dead weight in every COMM=SPI image.
findings.impact: Unused code carried in all SPI builds; mild flash bloat and maintenance surface. Not a runtime hazard. Irrelevant to the sealed (UART) deployment which excludes the whole file.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function and its prototype, or if intended for future use, mark it clearly and add a unit test so it is at least validated. It is a verbatim copy of the AT-path converter (mgr_at_cmd_list_user_data.c:226) and carries the same partial-overwrite-on-failure behavior.

findings.location: mgr_spi_cmd_list_user_data.c:235-244 (missing guard) vs AT path mgr_at_cmd_list_user_data.c:192
findings.description: The SPI WRITETX path is missing the bit-length sanity check that the UART path enforces. WRITETXSIZE only validates `userTxPayloadSize <= USERDATA_TX_PAYLOAD_MAX_SIZE` (=51, line 148) and WRITETX re-validates against `sizeof(u8DataBuf)` (=51, line 206). But the real MAC limit is USERDATA_TX_DATAFIELD_SIZE=25 bytes / 200 bits (LDA2). A raw payload of 26..51 bytes passes both checks, sets u16DataBitLen = size*8 up to 408 bits (line 243-244), yet only 25 bytes are actually copied into the MAC event (loop bound sizeof(appEvtTx.data_ctxt.usrdata)=KNS_MAC_USRDATA_MAXLEN=25, line 251). The AT path guards with `if (u16UserDataBitlen <= USERDATA_TX_DATAFIELD_SIZE*8)`; the SPI path has no equivalent.
findings.impact: On SPI hosts, a 26-51 byte TX request yields an event whose declared bitlen (>200) is inconsistent with the 25 bytes carried -> the Kineis encoder either rejects the frame (silent TX failure reported only via async MAC_STATUS) or, worse, transmits a frame built from declared-but-not-supplied length. Silent corruption / wasted TX. SPI-build only; sealed UART deploy unaffected.
findings.recommendation: Before line 243, reject when userTxPayloadSize > USERDATA_TX_DATAFIELD_SIZE (25), returning ERROR_INVALID_USER_DATA_LENGTH, mirroring the AT path. Tighten the WRITETXSIZE bound (line 148) to the same 25-byte limit since SPI carries raw bytes, not ASCII-hex.

findings.description: Neither handler validates that the frame actually carried the bytes it reads. WRITETXSIZE reads rx->data[1] and rx->data[2] with no check that the request data_len >= 2 (dispatcher sets rxBuf.size = req->data_len+1 at mgr_spi_cmd.c:156 but it is never consulted here). WRITETX copies `userTxPayloadSize` bytes from rx->data[1+idx] (line 236) without verifying the current WRITE_TX frame's data_len covers that many bytes. userTxPayloadSize was latched by a *separate prior* SPI transaction, so a master that sets size=50 then sends a WRITE_TX frame with only e.g. 5 payload bytes will copy 45 bytes of stale rxBuf content into the TX payload.
findings.impact: No buffer overflow (rxBuf is 256 B and indices stay <= 51), but silent transmission of stale/garbage bytes when the master under-fills a WRITE_TX frame, or a zero MSB assumed when WRITE_TX_SIZE is short. Corrupts the over-air Argos frame without any error to the host. SPI-build only.
